metadata.title: How Tax Lien Investing Actually Works
metadata.author: Lien Ledger
metadata.shortDescription:
Most people think tax lien investing means 18% returns and houses for pennies. Here's how tax lien investing actually works — and why some investors happily bid 0.25%.

In this video: what a tax lien certificate is, how state interest rates work (Florida, Arizona, New Jersey, Iowa), premium bidding vs bidding the rate down, redemption periods, why only about 1% of liens ended in foreclosure in Washington D.C.'s data, Florida's 5% minimum rule, tax deeds, the Tyler v. Hennepin County Supreme Court case, and the real risks.

Chapters
0:00 Hook
0:30 What a tax lien really is
1:25 The rates (and the catch)
2:48 Who actually gets paid
4:28 Florida's 5% rule
5:47 When nobody pays
7:35 Is it worth it?
8:14 Outro

Sources
- Florida Statutes §197.472 (redemption, 5% minimum): https://m.flsenate.gov/Statutes/197.472
- Florida Statutes §197.502 (tax deed application): https://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2015/197.502
- Leon County Tax Collector — Tax Sale FAQ: https://www.leontaxcollector.net/Investors/Tax-Sale-FAQ
- D.C. OCFO report on tax sales 2003–2012: https://cfo.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/ocfo/publication/attachments/OIO-13-2-18-A-OTR_0.pdf
- Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023): https://imla.org/2023/05/tyler-v-hennepin-county/

This video is for educational purposes only and is not financial, legal or tax advice. Rules vary by state and county — always check your local statutes and county tax collector.

investors can bid as low as a quarter of
1% interest
on a stranger's unpaid property taxes.
That sounds crazy. Most tax lien videos
promise you 18% returns,
but that tiny bid can earn far more than
it looks.
By the end of this video, you'll
understand exactly why and how tax liens
really work.
Let's start with the basics. Every year,
some property owners don't pay their
property taxes.
That's a real problem for the county.
Schools, roads, police, and fire
departments run on that money.
So in many states, the county doesn't
wait years to collect. It sells the debt
instead.
Here's how it works. Say a homeowner
owes $2,000 in back taxes. You pay that
amount to the county.
In return, you get a certificate. That's
the tax lien.
The owner still owns the home. They
still live in it. Nothing changes for
them yet.
But now, to clear that debt, they have
to pay you back plus interest.
And that interest rate isn't set by a
bank. It's set by state law,
which means it can be surprisingly high.
So how high are we talking? Different
states, wildly different numbers.
In Florida, the maximum is 18% a year.
In Arizona, it's 16%. In New Jersey, 18.
And in Iowa, it's 24% a year. That's 2%
every single month.
Compare that to a typical savings
account, and you can see why people get
excited.
But here's the catch. These are maximum
rates. You don't automatically get them
Because liens are sold at auction, and
auctions mean competition.
States use different systems. In some,
like New Jersey, investors bid a
premium.
You pay extra cash on top of the lien to
win it, and that extra cash cuts into
your return.
In others, like Florida and Arizona,
investors bid the interest rate down.
In Florida, bidding opens at 18% and
drops in steps of a quarter point.
The lowest rate wins, and when lots of
investors want the same lien,
that rate can collapse towards zero.
So why would anyone accept almost
nothing? Hold that thought. We'll get
there.
First, you need to understand the most
important word in tax lien investing,
redemption.
Redemption is when the owner pays off
the debt plus the interest they owe you.
They get a deadline to do it. That's
called the redemption period.
Depending on the state, it's usually
somewhere between 1 and 3 years,
sometimes as short as 6 months.
And here's what surprises most
beginners. The owner almost always pays.
Industry sources commonly claim that
more than 95% of liens get redeemed.
Why so high? A lien is attached to the
property. Owners don't want to lose
their home over a tax bill.
And mortgage lenders can step in and pay
it to protect their loan.
Official data tells a similar story.
Washington, D.C. reviewed 10 years of
its tax sales.
Out of 9,395
properties, 70% were redeemed.
16% were canceled. 13% were still in
progress.
And just 1% ended in foreclosure.
So if you're dreaming about getting a
house for a few thousand dollars,
the math says that's not what usually
happens.
In reality, a tax lien investor is
basically a lender.
You front the money and you get paid
back with interest,
which brings us back to that quarter of
1 % bid.
Florida has a rule that changes
everything.
It's in state law, section 197.472.
When a lien is redeemed, the investor
earns at least 5 % of the lien's face
value.
Even if they bid a lower rate, that's
the mandatory minimum.
There's one exception. If you bid 0 %,
you get no minimum at all.
So let's do the math. Say you buy a
$1,000 lien at a quarter of 1 %.
3 months later, the owner pays it off.
At a quarter % a year, your interest
would be less than $1.
But the 5 % minimum kicks in. You get
$50 instead.
$50 in 3 months. Annualize that and it's
roughly 20 %.
That 's why investors bid so low.
They're betting the owner pays quickly.
And that 's why so many bids pile up
just above zero.
But if the owner waits 2 years, that
same lien earns about 5 % total over 2
years.
Same lien, same bid, completely
different result. Timing is everything.
Now what about that 1 %? What happens
when the owner never pays?
In Florida, after about 2 years, you can
apply for a tax deed.
That forces the property to auction, but
you can't wait forever. If you don't
apply within seven years, your
certificate expires.
And applying isn't free.
You may have to pay off other liens on
the property plus fees and a title
search.
Even then, you're not guaranteed the
house. Other bidders can outbid you at
the deed sale.
If they do, you're typically paid back
from the proceeds.
And the rules got stricter. In 2023,
the U.S. Supreme Court decided Tyler
versus Hennepin County.
A Minnesota County sold a woman's condo
over a $15,000 tax debt.
And kept the difference. The court ruled
unanimously that the extra equity
belongs to the owner.
So the idea of grabbing a full house for
the price of its back taxes.
That's on much shakier legal ground
today.
Then there are the other risks. Some
liens sit on properties nobody wants.
Think vacant lots or damaged buildings.
Environmental problems can turn a
property into a liability instead of an
asset.
Bankruptcy can freeze the process and
delay your payout for years.
Your money is locked up. You can't
always cash out a lien whenever you
want.
And the interest you earn is generally
taxed as ordinary income.
So is tax lien investing worth it?
Here's the honest version.
It's not a shortcut to cheap houses.
It's a way to earn interest backed by
real property.
It rewards research. Check every
property before you bid. Read your
state's rules.
Many counties now run their auctions
online, so you can research and bid from
home. But that also means more
competition.
Start small in one county and learn how
it's auction works.
And never bid on a lien you wouldn't be
comfortable owning.
So remember, the 18% is a ceiling, not a
promise. The real game is the rules and
the timing.
Next, I'll break down tax deeds where
you bid on the property itself.
Subscribe so you don't miss it.
This video is for education only. It's
not financial advice.

Out of 9,395 properties, 70% were redeemed. 16% were canceled. 13% were still in progress. And just 1% ended in foreclosure. 1 %. So if you're dreaming about getting a house for a few thousand dollars, the math says that's not what usually happens. In reality, a tax lien investor is basically a lender. You front the money and you get paid back with interest, which brings us back to that quarter of 1 % bid. Florida has a rule that changes everything. It's in state law, section 197.472. When a lien is redeemed, the investor earns at least 5 % of the lien's face value. Even if they bid a lower rate, that's the mandatory minimum. There's one exception. If you bid 0 %, you get no minimum at all. So let's do the math. Say you buy a $1,000 lien at a quarter of 1 %. 3 months later, the owner pays it off. At a quarter % a year, your interest would be less than $1. But the 5 % minimum kicks in. You get $50 instead. $50 in 3 months. Annualize that and it's roughly 20 %. That 's why investors bid so low. They're betting the owner pays quickly. And that 's why so many bids pile up just above zero. But if the owner waits 2 years, that same lien earns about 5 % total over 2 years. Same lien, same bid, completely different result. Timing is everything. Now what about that 1 %? What happens when the owner never pays? In Florida, after about 2 years, you can apply for a tax deed. That forces the property to auction, but you can't wait forever. If you don't apply within seven years, your certificate expires. And applying isn't free. You may have to pay off other liens on the property plus fees and a title search. Even then, you're not guaranteed the house. Other bidders can outbid you at the deed sale. If they do, you're typically paid back from the proceeds. And the rules got stricter. In 2023, the U.S. Supreme Court decided Tyler versus Hennepin County. A Minnesota County sold a woman's condo for $40,000 over a $15,000 tax debt. And kept the difference. The court ruled unanimously that the extra equity belongs to the owner. So the idea of grabbing a full house for the price of its back taxes. That's on much shakier legal ground today. Then there are the other risks. Some liens sit on properties nobody wants. Think vacant lots or damaged buildings. Environmental problems can turn a property into a liability instead of an asset. Bankruptcy can freeze the process and delay your payout for years. Your money is locked up. You can't always cash out a lien whenever you want. And the interest you earn is generally taxed as ordinary income. So is tax lien investing worth it? Here's the honest version. It's not a shortcut to cheap houses. It's a way to earn interest backed by real property. It rewards research. Check every property before you bid. Read your state's rules. Many counties now run their auctions online, so you can research and bid from home. But that also means more competition. Start small in one county and learn how it's auction works. And never bid on a lien you wouldn't be comfortable owning. So remember, the 18% is a ceiling, not a promise. The real game is the rules and the timing. Next, I'll break down tax deeds where you bid on the property itself. Subscribe so you don't miss it. This video is for education only. It's not financial advice.

Florida is one of the best states to invest in and every real estate investor knows it! But can the same be said if you're looking into tax liens & deeds? In this video, I'll talk all about how property taxes work in this state and teach you step by step how to buy tax lien certificates in Florida!

Watch my FREE video to learn more about tax lien investing:
https://higginsmethod.com/

Watch And Enjoy!
Saen Higgins

Key Moments In This Episode
========================
00:00 Intro & Summary
01:52 What Florida Is Like
02:46 How Florida Handles Tax Delinquent Properties
03:57 What Happens After The Redemption Period In Florida
05:58 How Florida Sells Tax Lien Certificates
07:03 How The Bidding Process Works In Florida
08:08 How Tax Deed Sales Work In Florida
08:53 What To Understand About Tax Lien Investing
09:53 Learn More About Tax Liens & Deeds

Visit our website for more info:

→ How properties sell for 10-20 cents on the dollar at tax deed auctions

→ How I bought a $300,000 New York property with 30% down on a credit card

metadata.shortDescription:
⚖️ Should a county be allowed to keep the profit when it sells your home over unpaid taxes? The Supreme Court said no, 9 to 0. What do you think? 👇

Tax foreclosure and the surplus a county keeps, through one Supreme Court case. In Minneapolis, Geraldine Tyler owed about $2,300 in property taxes. With interest and penalties, the debt grew to about $15,000. The county took her condo, sold it for $40,000, and kept everything. In 2023 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that keeping the surplus was a taking. What the case changed for owners and heirs, what to ask the county treasurer in writing, and three questions to check in your state.

⚖️ General information, not legal advice. State laws vary. We don't buy houses and we don't take cases: we show you the rules, and where to check them.

metadata.title: Tyler v. Hennepin County and the Impact on Nebraska Tax Sales
metadata.author: Tax Sale Resources
metadata.shortDescription:
Tax Sale Resources CEO Brian Seidensticker sat down with Greg Scaglione, the attorney representing Continental Resources, to discuss the ongoing case and the tax sale situation in Nebraska. Greg discussed the arguments from both sides of the issue and the ramifications for investors in the state.

For a complete write-up of the discussion check out our blog at https://www.taxsaleresources.com/blog.

Check out https://www.taxsaleresources.com for all the resources needed to successfully grow your tax sale investment portfolio.
--

00:00:00 - Tax Sale Industry Update
00:03:18 - The US Supreme Court Case Update
00:06:33 - Argument over Equity in Tax Certificate Statutes
00:09:47 - The Benefit of Tax Certificates in Nebraska
00:12:42 - The small fraction of sold leans that result in foreclosure
00:15:23 - 2023 Nebraska Tax Certificate Issues
00:18:33 - The Future of Debated Topics

metadata.title: The Equity the County Kept
metadata.author: Community Living HQ
metadata.shortDescription:
Geraldine Tyler owed about $2,300 in property taxes. With interest and penalties, that grew to $15,000. Hennepin County foreclosed, sold her Minneapolis condo for $40,000 — and kept the entire $25,000 left over after her debt was paid. She received nothing. This was legal under Minnesota law at the time.

This video traces how property-tax foreclosure actually works, why the "keep the surplus" practice existed, and what happened when Tyler took her case to the Supreme Court — which ruled unanimously in 2023 that keeping value beyond a tax debt violates the Constitution's Takings Clause. It also covers what that ruling left unresolved, how states have responded unevenly since, and the still-unfolding 2026 sequel: a new Supreme Court ruling on how surplus value should actually be measured, and a Michigan court decision showing how procedural deadlines can erase even a constitutionally recognized right.

Chapters
00:00 Intro
01:01 Chapter 1: How Property-Tax Foreclosure Works
02:02 Chapter 2: Why the System Existed
03:03 Chapter 3: Who Absorbs the Loss
04:05 Chapter 4: Tyler Reaches the Supreme Court
05:06 Chapter 5: What Tyler Required and Left Open
06:06 Chapter 6: States Respond Unevenly
07:08 Chapter 7: The 2026 Sequel
08:16 Chapter 8: The Details Become the Battleground
09:17 Final Thoughts

🔔 Subscribe to Community Living for practical homeowner education — no drama, just the facts.

Sources referenced: *Tyler v. Hennepin County*, 598 U.S. 631 (2023); *Pung v. Isabella County*, No. 25-95 (decided June 23, 2026); *In re Petition of State Treasurer for Foreclosure for Unpaid Tax* (Mich. Ct. App., June 18, 2026); Minnesota Laws 2024, chapters 113 and 127; Maine PL 2024, chapter 640; Massachusetts General Laws chapter 60; and Nebraska Revised Statute § 77-1838.

metadata.title: 6 Ways to Invest in Tax Deeds and Tax Liens (Florida Examples)
metadata.author: The Jackie Jackson | Tax Deed & Real Estate Coach
metadata.shortDescription:
There are 6 ways to invest in tax deeds and tax liens, and only some of them involve bidding at an auction. In this video, I explain each one using Florida examples from Citrus County: the tax deed auction, contacting the owner before the auction, surplus overages, the lands available list, the tax lien certificate auction, and tax lien certificates the county still holds.

My history is in sales, finance, and banking, and I've been buying investment property since 2006. Bidding at the tax deed auction is the way most people know. You research the properties before the sale, and if you're the successful bidder, you're issued a deed. I've bought a lot of properties this way.

If you're not keen on the competitive bidding, you can contact the owner before the auction. The county's list normally has the owner's information. You might make a cash offer or help them redeem the property and get it taken off the list, so you come up with a solution together. Follow your state's rules and the calling laws when you reach out to owners.

Surplus overages are the money a property sells for above the opening bid. A lot of times, former owners don't know that money is available or that they can claim it, so some investors built a business helping them collect it for a fee. I also explain escheatment, which is what can happen to surplus that nobody claims. Those rules depend on the state.

In Florida, properties that get no bids at the tax deed auction go on a lands available list that the public can buy from. Contact the county for an actual payoff amount before you buy.

Tax lien certificates work differently. You don't get the property. You earn a rate of interest. In Florida, each county's tax collector holds a tax certificate sale for the year's delinquent taxes, and anyone can buy a county-held certificate that didn't sell.

I'm thrilled to have my good friend Ted Thomas on the show. Ted is a maestro in tax liens and tax deeds, an area of real estate investing with many fascinating parallels to the land flipping business—with a few important differences.

Today, we will explore the ins and outs of tax lien and tax-defaulted property investing. Ted is going to share his decades of experience in this niche and the exact strategies he uses to find and close these deals.

Whether you're an experienced real estate investor looking to expand your portfolio or you're just getting started and eager to learn, there's a ton to unpack here. Ted's expertise will shed light on the strategies, potential pitfalls, and the strategies needed to succeed in this complex yet rewarding space.

metadata.title: Bankruptcy Court Refuses to Award Damages for Automatic Stay Violation
metadata.author: Personal Bankruptcy Law Atlanta
metadata.shortDescription:
People file bankruptcy to obtain protection from creditors.  The automatic stay set out in Bankruptcy Code section 362 expressly prohibits creditors from starting or continuing collection or foreclosure actions and allows aggrieved debtors to sue for money damages.

In the case of Lodge v. Kondaur Capital and McCalla Raymer, however, the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the decision of a federal district court denying damages to a debtor despite an undisputed violation of the stay by a mortgage company and its attorneys.

In this video I explain why the 11th Circuit ruled as it did and what this decision means to you if you have suffered economic or emotional damage by a creditor.

Want more information about personal bankruptcy in the Atlanta area?  Visit my web site at http://www.atlanta-bankruptcy-attorney.com or call my office at 770-393-4985.

Jonathan Ginsberg
Ginsberg Law Offices
Atlanta bankruptcy law
770-393-4985

# The Mortgage Ledger: The Bankruptcy Gauntlet
## Day 01: The Automatic Stay Guillotine: Stopping Foreclosure with Hours to Spare

Welcome to **Day 01** of **The Bankruptcy Gauntlet**, an intensive investigative documentary series from **The Mortgage Ledger**.

In this episode, our investigative team—**Elena Vance**, **Julian Drake**, **Sophia Brooks**, and case witness **Marcus Vance**—dissect the statutory and accounting machinery governing this critical phase of mortgage bankruptcy.

---

### ⏱️ CHAPTER TIMESTAMPS:
- **00:00** - The Injunction Shield: 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)
- **00:29** - The PACER Timestamp vs. The County Clock
- **00:54** - Void vs. Voidable: The Doctrine of Total Invalidity
- **01:22** - The Servicer's Emergency Intake Playbook
- **01:46** - Marcus Vance: The Eve-of-Sale Scramble
- **02:12** - The Teeth: 11 U.S.C. § 362(k) Sanctions
- **02:45** - Community Dilemma: Post-Petition Harassment
- **03:06** - Day One Wrap-Up & Tomorrow's Episode Preview

---

### 📚 KEY STATUTES & PRECEDENTS COVERED:
- **11 U.S.C. § 362(a)**
- **11 U.S.C. § 362(k)**
- **In re Schwartz, 954 F.2d 569**
- **In re Soares, 107 F.3d 969**

---

### 💬 COMMUNITY QUESTION:
Now, let us turn to our community. If you filed for bankruptcy and your mortgage servicer called you three days later demanding payment, would you hang up, call your attorney to file an adversary complaint for contempt, or notify the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau? Tell us in the comments how you would enforce your statutory rights.

Drop your perspective in the comments below!

---
*Disclaimer: The Mortgage Ledger is produced for educational and informational purposes only. Consult a licensed bankruptcy attorney in your jurisdiction for guidance regarding specific mortgage accounts or legal proceedings.*

Rosa owed $48,000 after her bakery closed, and the collector had already sued her. Then she made one phone call, to a bankruptcy lawyer. We also break down Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13, the timing mistakes that cost people money, why paying back family right before filing can backfire, which debts survive bankruptcy, and the myths that keep people stuck.

segments.text: Rosa made one phone call to a bankruptcy
lawyer. That afternoon, her lawyer filed
her case in federal court, and by the
next morning, every collector chasing
her had to stop. But, there's something

in her driveway. Here's every step of
bankruptcy, from the filing to the fresh
start. First, how Rosa got here. For 6
years, she ran a small bakery. When it
closed, she was left with $48,000
in credit cards and personal loans she'd
used to keep it alive. The calls never
stopped. And last month, one of the
collectors sued her. So, what is
bankruptcy? It's a federal court process
that lets people who can't pay their
debts either wipe out many of them or
pay them back under a court-approved
plan. For most people, it comes down to
two types. Chapter 7 is the fast one. It
usually takes a few months, and many
debts are simply erased. Chapter 13 is a
repayment plan that lasts 3 to 5 years,
and it can let people keep property
they'd otherwise lose. Step one, the
class. Before anyone can file, they
generally have to take a credit
counseling course from an approved
agency, often online, within the 6
months before filing. It covers
budgeting and alternatives to
bankruptcy. Rosa takes it on her laptop
that same afternoon and gets a
certificate her lawyer files with the
case. Then, Rosa gathers everything: pay
stubs, tax returns, bank statements, a
list of every debt she owes, and
everything she owns. Her lawyer warns
her about one thing right away.
Everything has to be listed. Hiding
money or property in a bankruptcy isn't
just a mistake. It can be a federal
crime. And every creditor goes on the
list, even a friend or a family member
she owes. People can't pick which debts
to include, but after the case, Rosa is
free to voluntarily repay anyone she
wants. Her lawyer also gives her a
warning about the weeks before filing.
Running up credit cards on luxury items
or taking big cash advances right before
bankruptcy can lead a creditor to ask
the judge not to wipe out those debts.
Step two, which chapter? To file chapter
seven, most people have to pass
something called the means test. It
starts by comparing your household
income to the typical income for a
household your size in your state. If
you're below that line, you can usually
file chapter seven. If you're above it,
a longer calculation looks at your
expenses to see whether you could afford

Learn about the quiet title process, its importance for tax lien auction winners, and the role of counties in addressing title defects. Understand the costs, need for attorney expertise, and Ted's experiences. Explore the necessity of title insurance, alternative selling strategies, and the legalities involved, all aimed at maximizing profits in real estate. - GIFT: https://tedthomas.com/ytl-1005/

Video Highlights:
 Quiet title is a lawsuit to settle property claims, but the process is handled by an attorney hired by the property owner.
🕒 The process typically takes 3 to 6 months and costs $3,000 to $5,000, potentially more if there are multiple claims to settle.
💼 Quiet title applies to all types of properties, including agricultural, commercial, and residential.
💰 Buyers at tax defaulted auctions will require a clear title, often through a quiet title action, before purchasing a property.
⚖️ Options for selling tax delinquent property without completing a quiet title include selling on contract with an installment plan.

metadata.shortDescription:
A plain-language look at how to clear a title in Texas: the liens that attach to property, how priority works, why problems surface at closing, and how quiet title suits help. Texas law, explained in plain language.

Read the full article:
https://www.stackedlegal.com/post/how-to-clear-title-texas-liens?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=how-to-clear-title-texas-liens

Get Texas Real Estate Liens and Title Disputes:
https://www.stackedlegal.com/books/texas-real-estate-liens-guide?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=how-to-clear-title-texas-liens

In this lesson:
- Mortgage, tax and judgment liens arise in different ways
- First in time, first in right, with key exceptions
- A Texas homestead is shielded from most forced sales
- Title searches often surface old claims at closing
- Quiet title and lien removal routes each have limits

metadata.title: HOA Liens Explained – Can They Take Your House?
metadata.author: HOA Insights
metadata.shortDescription:
What if a letter in your mailbox could cost you your house? Not a mortgage. Not a bank. Your homeowners association.

In this video, HOA Insights explains in plain English what an HOA lien is, how unpaid fees become a lien, the difference between an assessment lien and a fine lien, and when a lien can lead to foreclosure — judicial vs non-judicial — plus what you can do if you get a lien notice: read the notice, check your CC&Rs, ask for a full accounting in writing, and don't ignore deadlines.

Has your HOA ever sent you a letter you did not understand? Tell us in the comments.

Subscribe to HOA Insights — every week we break down another HOA fee, rule, or right in plain English, before it costs you money.

This video is general information only. It is not legal advice. HOA laws vary by state, and your community's rules matter too. If you need advice about your own situation, talk to a licensed attorney or a qualified professional in your state.

segments.text: What if a letter in your mailbox could
cost you your house? Not a mortgage, not
a bank, your Homeowners Association. You
paid for your home, you pay your
mortgage on time,
but one unpaid HOA bill can turn into a
lien,
and a lien can lead to foreclosure.
Can an HOA take your house?
In some states and in some situations,
yes, it can try, but it does not happen
overnight and it [clears throat] does
not happen without warning. Today we
explain how a lien works step by step in
plain English, so you know what to watch
for and what to do if it ever happens to
you.
First, what is a lien?
A lien is a legal claim against your
home.
It is a public record that says you owe
money and that the money is tied to your
property.
It does not mean you have lost your
home.
It means the debt is attached to it.
When you buy a home in an HOA community,
you agree to follow the community rules
and to pay your dues. Those dues are
called assessments. They pay for shared
costs like roads, pools, and
landscaping.
The agreement you signed, usually the CC
and Rs, gives the HOA the right to
collect those dues, and in many
communities, the right to place a lien
if dues go unpaid.
The HOA does not need to take your house
to place a lien. It only needs to record
the claim.
Once recorded, it becomes part of your
property's public record,
and that can make it harder to sell your
home or to refinance it
because a buyer or a lender will see
that money is owed.
How does a miss payment turn into a
lien?
It usually happens in stages, and the
HOA is generally required to follow a
process.
It starts with a missed assessment.
Maybe you forgot or money was tight that
month. At first, the HOA sends a
reminder, then it may add late fees and
interest if the community rules allow
it. Those charges can grow over time,
which is why a small missed payment can
become a much larger balance if it is
ignored.
If the balance stays unpaid, the HOA may
send a formal demand letter explaining
what is owed and giving you a chance to
pay or to ask questions.
After that, if the debt is still unpaid,
the HOA may record a lien against your
property.
The exact steps and notices depend on
your state's laws and your community's
documents. The key point is this. A lien
is not a surprise ending. It is the
result of a process.
And at almost every step, there is a
chance to act, to pay, to ask for a
payment plan,
or to dispute a charge you believe is
wrong. Not all HOA debts are treated the
same. It helps to know the difference
between two common kinds of liens.
The first is an assessment lien. This
comes from unpaid regular dues or from a
special assessment, a one-time charge
for a major repair or project.
Assessment liens are the most common
kind, and in many states, they carry the
strongest collection powers because dues
are the HOA's main source of funding.
The second is a fine lien. This comes
from fines for rule violations, like an
unapproved fence or parking in the wrong
place.
In some states, an HOA can place a lien
for fines. In other states, it cannot,
or it can only do so under limited
conditions. Your CCNRs and state law
decide which kind of debt can become a
lien. That difference matters because it
affects your options. An assessment debt
is usually harder to dispute than a fine
because the dues are a clear obligation.
A fine can sometimes be challenged if
the rule was not applied fairly
or if the HOA did not follow its own
hearing process.
Now the question everyone asks, can a
lien lead to foreclosure?
In some states, yes. In others, the path
is much harder or it works differently.
In some states, the HOA must go to court
to foreclose.
That is called judicial foreclosure.
In other states, the law allows a
non-judicial foreclosure,
which means the HOA can move toward a
sale without a full court case as long
as it follows the notice and procedure
rules set by state law. Either way,
foreclosure is usually a last step, not
a first step. It generally comes after
months of unpaid dues, notices, and a
recorded lien.
How much must be owed and how much
notice is required all vary by state.
Some states also give homeowners a right
to cure the debt, meaning you can pay
what is owed plus allowed costs and stop
the foreclosure.
Do not assume a lien means you will lose
your home tomorrow and do not ignore the
letters. The earlier you act, the more
options you usually have.
So what can you do if you get a lien
notice or if you're falling behind?
Start with these steps.
First, read the notice carefully. Find
out exactly what you owe and whether it
is for assessments, fines, or both.
Second, read your CC&Rs or ask someone
qualified to help you read them.
Look for the collection policy and any
right to a hearing or payment plan.
Third, contact the HOA or its management
company in writing.
Ask for a full accounting of the debt.
If you can pay, ask about a payment
plan.
If you believe a charge is wrong,
dispute it in writing and keep copies of
everything.
Fourth, do not ignore court papers or
deadlines. If you receive anything that
looks like a legal notice, take it
seriously and get help quickly.
A housing counselor, legal aid office,
or attorney in your state can explain
your options. And finally, stay in
communication.
Silence is what turns a small problem
into a large one.
A homeowner who responds early and keeps
records is in a much stronger position.
A lien is serious, but it is not the end
of the
It is a warning
and a process. And you have rights at
every step.
The homeowners who get into the most
trouble are not the ones who owe the
most.
They are the ones who did not know what
a lien was until it was already
recorded.
If this helped, subscribe to HOA
Insights.
Every week we break down another HOA
rule, fee, or right in plain English
before it costs you money.
And tell us in the comments, has your
HOA ever sent you a letter you did not
understand?
This video is general information only.
It is not legal advice. HOA laws vary by
state and your community's rules matter
too.
If you need advice about your own
situation, talk to a licensed attorney
or a qualified professional in your
state.
Thank you for watching and we will see
you in the next one.
Uh

metadata.author: Alex Goldovsky
metadata.shortDescription:
Description

Podcast EP 59: Tax Liens, HOA Liens & Title Traps Every Investor Must Know

In this special episode, Alex joins Logan Fullmer's podcast to discuss one of the most overlooked aspects of real estate investing: title risk.

Drawing on nearly two decades of experience building ProTitleUSA into one of the nation's leading title research providers, Alex shares real-world examples of how investors can identify hidden risks, negotiate complex liens, and uncover opportunities others miss.

From tax liens and HOA super-priority liens to IRS releases, foreclosure strategy, title curative work, and real estate fraud schemes, this conversation is packed with practical lessons for investors, note buyers, and distressed asset professionals.

🔍 Topics Covered
00:00 Intro Music
00:09 Introduction to Alex Goldovsky & ProTitleUSA
02:45 How ProTitleUSA Started
05:20 Why Title Reports Matter for Investors
08:10 Tax Liens, HOA Liens & Foreclosure Auctions
12:05 Mortgage Priority & Hidden Investor Risks
16:25 Negotiating IRS, State Tax & Government Liens
20:10 Municipal Liens, Code Violations & Permit Issues
24:20 Why Professional Title Research Matters
28:50 Inside ProTitleUSA’s National Search Operation
33:30 Bulk Reports, Dashboards & Curative Services
37:45 Old Mortgages, Releases & Title Cleanup
41:15 Blockchain, Digital Mortgages & Future of Title
44:10 Fraud Schemes, Fake Appraisals & Red Flags
46:10 Final Advice & How to Connect with Alex

👉 Like, comment, and subscribe for more conversations on real estate investing, distressed assets, title research, and mortgage industry trends.

Explore the basics of tax liens and deeds, particularly over-the-counter properties. Learn about misconceptions, property assessment, the role of realtors in tax deeds, and challenges in these deals. Understand the value of expert coaching, hear success stories in property flipping, and access a guide to property lists. -GIFT: https://tedthomas.com/ytl-27678/

Video Highlights:
💡 Over-the-counter tax deeds are properties that were not sold at the tax delinquent auction and are held by the county.
💰 These properties can offer a great opportunity for investment, despite being rejected or abandoned by previous owners.
🏛️ Different counties may refer to these properties using various names, such as scavenger list, leftover lands list, or strike off list.
🏠 Realtors may be hesitant to work with over-the-counter properties due to potential issues with the condition of the property and the title, as well as the lack of commission.
🤝 Working with professionals, like coaches or attorneys, can help navigate the challenges and maximize the potential of over-the-counter tax deed opportunities.

He teaches how to create wealth with minimum risk with easy-to-learn methods. Ted’s strategies developed over decades of successful real estate investing can help everyone. From regular hard-working families to senior citizens, to young families and professionals.

Ted chose to teach Tax Lien Certificate and Tax Defaulted Property investing because it is Certain, Predictable, and Secure. Industry insiders consider Ted Thomas to be America’s Tax Lien Certificate and Tax Deed Authority. Before investing in tax lien certificates or tax deeds, it is important to seek professional advice from attorneys, financial advisors, and CPAs. Whenever earnings are shown, it should be noted that the earnings reported are likely to be higher than the average student may achieve. Tax-defaulted real estate carries risks, and there is no financial guarantee offered or implied.

metadata.shortDescription:
http://taxsalesupport.com/  This is a replay of our weekly training held on 12/28/16, we talk about real estate investing through Tax Liens and Tax Foreclosures (or Tax Deeds).  Tax liens and deeds are simply enforcement systems created by state law to ensure that property taxes are paid.  In this webinar we discuss different aspects of over the counter tax lien and tax deeds investing.   Earn high interest rate returns safely, or acquire property for pennies on the dollar.  Tax sales are the only investment a person needs. Investments range from $25 to $2.5 million dollars.  Get incredible returns while also having the highest degree of security.

Subscribe for more great videos, and to keep up to date on all the hottest Tax Lien & Deed investing strategies and upcoming auctions!

FREE GIFT: Are you new to Tax Sale Investing? Download our free eBook Series (as seen on TV) “Tax Lien Investor Secrets” at http://secretsoftaxlieninvesting.com ($29 Value). Plus check out the other free training and information available at Secrets of Tax Lien Investing. 

TSS MEMBERSHIP: Do you need additional tax sale training? Our Membership program starts at only $29 a month and comes with a 30-Day Money Back Guarantee! You won’t find a better value for tax sale education period. We provide the training books, auctions & OCT lists, weekly webinars and much more. Find out how you can become a Member at http://www.taxsalesupport.com 

SECONDARY MARKET: Don’t have time to attend the auctions yourself? You might be a good candidate for our Secondary Tax Lien & Deed Program. Learn about the Secondary Tax Lien/Deed Market at http://www.secondarytaxlien.com 

FOLLOW US ON SOCIAL MEDIA
TSS YouTube: http://www.youtube.com/channel/UCzobrs9J9VnxWrNDfxZtPug
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/TaxSaleSupport/
Twitter:  https://twitter.com/TaxSaleSupport1

THE BEST INVESTMENT PERIOD: You can safely earn Double Digit Returns on your money with Tax Liens, and acquire property for 10%-50% of Market Value through Tax Deed Foreclosures. Learn about the new Foreclosure Opportunity available to investors and the methods used to invest in real estate tax liens and tax deeds. Learn about Tax sale buying methods including live auctions, online auctions, over the counter investing and Bank Owned Secondary Tax Liens & Deeds.

OUR COMMITMENT: At Tax Sale Support we are committed to giving inventors the tools and knowledge to become successful with Tax Lien and Tax Deed Investing.  Tax Sale Support Founders Stephen Swenson and Shade Ferre have been teaching Tax Sale Investing strategies for over 20 years. Their strategies and techniques have been taught to over sixty thousand investors at seminars, coaching programs, online trainings and even on TV. You won’t find a better value for tax sale training then working with Stephen & Shades Team at Tax Sale Support. 

Thanks, Stephen & Shade

For more OTC tax lien/deed secrets, check the link in description—and SUBSCRIBE today

metadata.title: I Bought a Tax Lien. Where’s My House? | Beginner’s Guide New Edition Part 1
metadata.author: Ted Thomas
metadata.shortDescription:
Free Membership & Tools: https://TedThomas.com/ytl-260703.1 | Ted answers the questions most people ask first: what do you actually own, and can an ordinary person really do this? 

Watch the full series: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLLjU5Q-abnCw

What Part One Covers:
- What a tax lien certificate actually is: a piece of paper carrying the county's claim against the property, not ownership of the house or the land
- Why counties sell them at all, because the treasurer has to fund firefighters, school teachers, and county payroll on a budget that cannot wait for late payers
- Where the rate comes from: the state legislature sets the maximum and hands it to the treasurer. Florida up to 18%, Arizona 16%, Iowa 24%
- Interest states versus penalty states: Georgia pays a 20% penalty and Texas 25%, paid whether the owner redeems on day one or day three hundred
- Redemption windows by state, roughly two years in Florida and three years in Arizona, and why you still pay the following year's property taxes to hold your position
- Why you deal only with the county treasurer and never with the property owner
- How hedge funds and banks buy whole pages of certificates at a time, and where a small investor still has an edge
- What "secured" means in the eyes of the law, and why a tax lien certificate only clears when it gets paid or the process ripens all the way to a tax deed sale
- A client example from the video: about $100,000 in certificates on country club homes that redeemed in roughly 30 days at a 5% return. That is one example, not a promise
- Why this is not a get rich quick business, and what the work actually looks like

Part Two picks up where this leaves off: how to actually research a property before you bid.

Video Highlights:
0:00 - Why Getting Educated Comes Before Buying Any Tax Lien Certificate
0:38 - Paying Someone Else's Property Taxes: What Is Really Happening
1:45 - Why Most People Never Hear About Tax Lien Certificates
2:58 - Who Actually Falls Behind On Property Taxes
4:57 - What A Tax Lien Certificate Is In Plain English
5:51 - Are You Buying Part Of The House Or Only A Claim
6:50 - Why The County Sells Instead Of Waiting For Payment
8:30 - Is The Interest Guaranteed, Or Mandated By State Law
10:37 - Benevolent States Versus Ruthless States
11:53 - Do Rates Vary By State: Florida 18%, Iowa 24%, Arizona 16%
12:55 - Can You Buy Tax Lien Certificates Outside Your Home State
13:27 - When Counties Hold Their Tax Lien Certificate Sales
14:45 - How Many Tax Lien Certificates You Can Buy At Once
15:33 - Competing Against Hedge Funds And Banks At Auction
15:51 - What Makes A Tax Lien Certificate Secured
19:17 - How Long Before A Tax Lien Certificate Redeems
20:40 - How Much Money A Beginner Actually Needs To Start
21:53 - Vacant Lots, Ranch Land, And Shopping Centers
24:05 - How To Start When You Do Not Live Near The Auction
25:27 - The Beginner Mistake That Loses Your Money
27:36 - Which States Sell Tax Lien Certificates And Which Sell Tax Deeds
28:31 - What Happens If The Property Owner Never Redeems
30:33 - Interest States Versus Penalty States: Georgia 20%, Texas 25%
33:10 - How Many States Use The Redeemable Penalty System
34:15 - What To Do If Your State Does Not Sell Tax Lien Certificates
37:00 - How To Avoid Scams And Buy Only Through The County
38:03 - Researching A County List Online And Bidding The Rate Down
41:09 - Why This Is Not A Get Rich Quick Business
44:36 - Why Education Is The Real Risk Control

I'm Ted Thomas. I've taught tax lien and tax deed investing for over 30 years. Before investing, seek professional advice. Results shown may exceed typical outcomes; all investing carries risk.

segments.text: How does a tax sale work in Illinois? In today's video, I'm going to talk to you about the several
different ways you can buy properties at tax sale auction in Illinois. Plus, I'm going to give you
an insider way to get properties where you don't have to attend the auction and you don't have to
go through the complexity, because, as you're going to see in Illinois, buying a tax sale can
be complicated because it involves things like redemption periods and special legal notices and
timing and things like that. So at the end, I'll show you a way to do that that is much simpler,
but because you asked about Illinois, let's get into the details of that.
The first thing to
know is that Illinois is a tax lien state, not a tax deed state. What that means is that what
you're buying at the auction is a lien against the property, and that lien carries an interest
rate of 18% so that can be a really good rate of return. But as with many things in Illinois,
it can get complicated. So the way that you bid is, it's called a bid down process. What it means
is that I bid 18% someone else says, well, I'll take 17% someone else says, I'll take 16% it keeps
going down until you get to the investor willing to take the least amount of money, and it can go,
and sometimes does go as low as 0% that's right, I said it 0% you say, Well, why would anybody want
to do that? And then we get into the next part about Illinois tax sales, and that is subsequent
taxes and the right to redeem. So what happens in Illinois when you get the tax lien certificate,
you're going to get interest when and if someone pays it, or you're eventually going to get the
property. But during the time when you hold the tax lien certificate, taxes are still
accumulating, so when the next tax bills come up, if the owner doesn't pay them, which you probably
won't, then you can pay those taxes, and you get to collect 12% interest on that money that you
invest. So what some tax lien investors are doing in Illinois is assuming that most people are going
to redeem, which is true. Most people are going to save their property from the tax man, so they are
going to pay the taxes. They're just going to pay them late, so when you pay the subsequent taxes,
you don't have to compete with other bidders where, you know, Fred's bidding, you know,
10% Lisa's bidding, 8% you know, and so on. Instead, in the subsequent taxes, because you hold
the first tax lien, you can pay the next year's taxes and get 12% which is a great return. Now,
if someone ultimately doesn't pay the taxes, and enough time goes by, then you're going to become
the owner of the property, as long as you follow an important process, and that process is called
giving out the 22 five notice. What this notice is, is a notice that the tax sale has happened to
the former owner and other stakeholders, letting them know, and it puts you in a position to later
get a deed. If you don't do this properly, meaning you get the timing wrong, or you don't do it at
all, then you won't be able to get a deed on the property and just have thrown away your money and
paid someone else's taxes, which is not a good thing. This notice is sent to the last assessee,
meaning the person who was on the tax record. So it's going to be the last owner of the property.
It's sent to them, and what it tells them is that the tax sale happened, that the tax lien was sold,
and the amount they need to pay to redeem the property. So it's notifying them,
and you need to do that within four months and 15 days of the tax sale. It's very important,
especially in Cook County, they require strict compliance with it. Other counties,
they require substantial compliance. You might get a little bit of leeway, but in all counties,
you do not want to have to be begging a judge to give you a break from you not doing your job. So
you need to make sure that that notice goes out, that it's perfect, and that's where my
next piece of advice is going to come. You really need to have an experienced attorney working with
you on these tax sales if you're going to be doing them. This is not the kind of thing to
go in as a complete do it yourself, or you need an experienced attorney. So the ways you can
find them pretty simple. Start doing some searches on Google for how tax sales work in Cook County,
and what you're going to find is you'll see some attorneys will put up articles on how tax sales
work, and educating would be investors on tax sales. That's a way that attorneys market their
services. And you know that that attorney wants to get clients in the tax sale arena,
and they're probably experienced in that arena, that's a good way to get yourself connected with
experienced counsel, because you need that in this business. Because in the tax sale business,
you have lots of issues that come up that need legal help. Sometimes you have people over gaming.
Other times you have just disputes with former owners. You have disputes with mortgage companies
and things like that. So you're going to need an attorney to guide you through this process,
not to discourage you. Can be a very proud. Profitable and great business to be in. It's just
that one of your team members is a talented and experienced state licensed attorney in Illinois
who's going to help you comply with, say, the 22 five notice. They're going to prepare that notice,
make sure it gets served on the appropriate people and be prepared to defend it if they need to. Now,
the redemption periods can be long, and let me explain what a redemption period is and why this
matters to you as a tax lien investor. So a redemption period is the time for someone to
pay the taxes and keep their property. So let's say you buy a property today. Let's say today,
just for simply sake, we're January 1. Then if it's a residential property, they have two and
a half years to redeem the property, meaning any time over the next two and a half years,
they can come pay the taxes, pay your interest and other expenses, and then they can get the
property back. And most people do redeem. That's why it's attractive to get the subsequent taxes,
meaning paying like, say, you bought it this year, and even at zero interest rate, when you buy next
year's taxes, and you get 12% of them and say that they stole our redeem they go another half a year,
and you buy those taxes, then you're going to collect 12% on one and a half years worth of
taxes, which can be substantial and can make up for the fact that on the first year taxes,
maybe you don't get anything so that can really make up for that. So subsequent taxes are a big
part of this, but you need to know about them, and you need to make sure you stay on top of it and
pay those taxes. You don't want another tax lien investor getting in front of you on that and also,
a good thing about tax sales in Illinois is that when the owner redeems, they have to redeem all
the taxes. They can't just redeem your year and then just keep struggling through the next
years. They have to get all of them. So if you invested in the second year of subsequent taxes,
and even third year subsequent taxes, then they have to redeem all of them at once, which is nice,
because it gives you a nice payout right then and there. And that is what's going to happen with
most of these properties. They will be redeemed. Occasionally you're going to get the deed to the
property. And when you get to the deed to the property, that can really be a big payday, because
you're going to get the deed for essentially the taxes that you paid, plus the subsequent taxes.
Let's say it's two, two and a half years worth of taxes. That can be really amazing, because taxes,
on average, are a little less than 2% of the property value per year. So if you got a property,
even if you paid three years worth of taxes, just to make it simple, that's probably 6% of
the property value, and you get the property free and clear of mortgages and most other liens. So
that can be really an amazing deal, but that's something that's going to happen occasionally.
Whenever you're investing in tax liens, it's not typically a play for the deed, it's typically a
play for interest, and occasionally you'll get a bonus of getting a deed. And when it comes to
getting the deed, you also have to file in court. You have to file a petition to get the deed, which
is why you're going to need your local attorney to help you. They can work you through that, as long
as they're experienced in tax sales. And when you get that deed, the property is yours just for the
little bit of taxes that you paid. Also understand that Cook County is a little bit stricter and a
little harder to deal with in the outer counties, which are not Cook County, those are a little bit
easier. Although Cook County, of course, being largest contains Chicago, that's going to be where
the most opportunity is. But you definitely need professional guidance in Cook County, and there's
going to be more competition there. That being said, there are a lot more properties too. So it
could be really good opportunity. I think overall, you can have good results in Illinois with tax
sales. But I also think for most people, there are simpler ways to do this business. And there's a
gentleman I ran into that came up with the best way to invest in tax deed properties that I've
seen, and that's essentially getting properties that have already been exposed to sale, but are
now sitting there on government lists because nobody bought them and they're just waiting to be
bought. They have those in Illinois. It's called the scavenger sale, which is, I did another video
on scavenger sale. You can look at my channel because I did a video on it, but this could be
a really great way to buy properties, because you don't have any competition, you don't have any
notices you have to file or figure out. You don't have redemption periods to deal with. Instead,
you just get properties. And literally, there are 10s of 1000s of properties out there that you can
choose from. And you really just look through the list and decide the ones you want, check them out,
and for the ones you want get them, typically, you get them for literally pennies on the dollar.
It's really amazing. To learn more about that you can click on the link down below this video down
there, it's my interview with Tony who came up with this whole process. He does it nationwide,
really, in its amazing process to acquire properties for literally pennies on the dollar,
without competition, without worrying about notices, without hiring attorneys all over the
place without getting into conflicts. So I really like that business model. I like it better than
than what we've been talking about today, which is sort of fighting it out with the hoi polloi to
get properties. It's good, you can do it, but I think it's much harder than it needs to be,
and I'd rather be able to focus on the business of Real Estate. Which is getting properties, fixing
them up, getting them occupied, getting them resold. And when you're battling out, you know,
did you send a notice at the right day or not? That's not going to push you in that direction.
So I think that what you should do from here is go click on that video. Go watch my 20 minute
interview with Tony. It's completely free. It's right here on YouTube, and learn about that way of
doing the business, I think is better than duking out at the auction. Although that being said,
I duked it out at auctions for many, many years. I discovered there are better ways later. So you
may want to duke it out for a while yourself, also with tax sales. If I can give you one other reason
why I think it's not the best option in tax sales, you don't get to inspect the property.
There's no open house. You just buy it. And a lot of times you're buying a little bit of a pig in
a poke because you can't see the inside of the property. And if you're buying a tax lien that
maybe you're going to get a deed three years from now, in a cold weather city like Chicago,
the condition of a house can can degrade greatly in two or three years from when you buy the tax
lien to when you get the property. So it can be a really difficult environment to work in,
and you have to be prepared for very heavy duty rehabs in that so I think that there are
better things to do than the tax lien sale in Illinois. So what you should do next is
go check out the interview I did with Tony, and that will show you a great path forward.

metadata.title: How to Check if a Tax Sale House Is Still There Before You Bid
metadata.author: Tax Sales Rebels
metadata.shortDescription:
Before bidding on an over-the-counter tax sale property, compare the county parcel record, property address, and current map imagery. A county record may identify a structure, but it does not confirm what is on the parcel today.

Start by matching the parcel details to the physical address, then check current map imagery for the same location. If the record, address, and imagery do not line up, keep researching before making a bidding decision.

This is a practical first step in Investigate the Asset. The goal is not to make a decision from one listing, but to build evidence before you bid.

Ever stare at a Tax Sale list filled with parcel numbers and legal descriptions and think, how do I actually find these properties? In this video, I’ll show you exactly how to take that text-based list and turn it into real, physical locations using GIS tools.

You’ll see my process for finding properties, understanding the data behind each one, and spotting great opportunities. If you’ve ever wanted to bridge the gap between what’s on paper and what’s in the real world, this walkthrough will change the way you research!

Want to learn more? Visit our comprehensive step-by-step training academy at http://www.TaxSaleAcademy.com

Actually, yes way. And that is exactly what we're going to explore today. Here is our road map. First, we'll break down the hidden IRS trap. Second, the 120-day redemption window. Third, the IRS reimbursement formula. Fourth, navigating those investor risks and finally, how to clear the title. Let's jump right in. Section one, the hidden IRS trap and those tricky post-sale risks. Buying distressed real estate is always a little bit of a gamble, but this specific risk hides deep down in the chain of title. See, when a delinquent taxpayer loses their home to a foreclosure, there's often a tangled web of debt attached to the property. If one of those debts happens to be a junior federal tax lien, meaning the previous owner owed money to the IRS. That lien might actually still haunt the property even after you win the auction and the gavel drops. The IRS doesn't just walk away simply because the bank foreclosed. And this brilliantly illustrates exactly why the IRS steps in. They're doing this to protect the government's interest. If a property gets auctioned off for pennies on the dollar, the IRS loses out on recovering the back taxes they're owed. So, they have this statutory power to basically buy the property back from the winning bidder, turn right around, and flip it themselves at a higher fair market value to pay off that taxpayer's liability. It's almost like the government is running its own real estate flipping side hustle. Moving right along to section two, the 120-day redemption window and the statutory timeline. So, how does the IRS actually pull off this maneuver? Well, it's called the right of redemption. If we translate the dense legal jargon of Internal Revenue Code Section 7425D into plain English, it's basically the government's absolute right to step directly into the shoes of the winning bidder at a foreclosure sale. Put simply, if they want the property, they can take it. Let's look at how this builds on a timeline because dates are literally everything here. For a non-judicial foreclosure sale to even affect a federal tax lien, the foreclosing entity, which is usually the bank, has to deliver a written notice to the IRS at least 25 days before the sale. Now, if the IRS doesn't get that 25-day notice, their tax lien survives the foreclosure completely intact. But, if they do get the notice, the lien is discharged and the clock starts on day zero, the day of the sale. From that exact moment, the IRS has exactly 120 days to decide if they want to redeem the property. But, wait. There's some fine print to pay attention to. While 120 days is the federal standard under Title 28 of the US Code, you always have to check your local laws. The rule is actually 120 days or the period allowable under state law, whichever is longer. So, depending on where you're buying, your waiting period could be even longer than 4 months. All right, section three, the IRS reimbursement formula, or how you get paid back. Let's say the IRS does decide to step in during that window, what happens to your money? Well, the good news is they don't just seize the house and leave you high and dry. They use a very strict statutory formula to pay you back. First, they'll reimburse you for the actual bid amount, which is the exact price you paid at the auction. On top of that, they tack on a 6% statutory interest rate calculated from the date of the sale. And finally, they add in any necessary expenses you incurred to secure and maintain the property while you owned it. When you break it down, the math actually feels quite accessible and pretty fair. But keep in mind, it's not purely a one-way street of additions. The IRS is going to make a few subtractions from your reimbursement, too. They will deduct any income you realize from the property. Like say you collected rent from a tenant during that 120-day window, they'll subtract that. And even if you just lived in the property yourself, they'll deduct the reasonable rental value for the time you were occupying it. Let's transition to section four, navigating the investor risks to protect your capital. This is absolutely crucial. What should a buyer do, and more importantly, what shouldn't they do during this waiting period? It all comes down to how the IRS defines necessary expenses. Things like casualty insurance, changing the locks, paying property taxes, or fixing a burst pipe, totally reimbursable. But remember those new kitchen cabinets you were so excited to rip out and replace? Yeah, the IRS is not legally obligated to reimburse you for cosmetic renovations, installing granite countertops, or putting in new hardwood floors. If you start your big cosmetic flip before that 120-day redemption window is fully closed, and the IRS decides to redeem the property, you lose all the money you dumped into those upgrades, every single cent. So you really just have to wait it out. But here's a nice little silver lining for you, 6%. Having your capital tied up for 4 months is incredibly frustrating for an investor, for sure. But, if the IRS does redeem the property, the money you parked in that house is earning a guaranteed 6% annual statutory interest rate. It's [snorts] a solid, guaranteed return while you just sit back and watch the clock. Plus, let's be honest, it's probably the one and only time in your life the IRS will happily pay you 6% interest. And that brings us to our final part, section five, clearing the title and removing the exception. Now, let's say you don't want to just sit around and wait. If you try to turn around and sell the property to a new buyer on day 30, you're going to hit a massive brick wall. For title professionals, this 120-day window is a critical insurability risk because the government could exercise its right and take back the title at literally any moment. A title company is going to mandate an exception on your title insurance, and no standard buyer's mortgage lender is ever going to fund a loan with that exception sitting on the title. It's just not going to happen. So, here is your highly actionable playbook to survive this process. Step one, always confirm the foreclosing bank actually delivered that 25-day notice to the IRS. If they didn't, you've got a much bigger headache on your hands. Step two, calculate your exact 120-day window based on the sale date. And step three, you either have to wait out the clock patiently, or you can proactively apply for a waiver of the redemption right. And here's the really cool part about that waiver. You don't always have to wait the full 4 months. You can submit an application to the IRS Collection Advisory Group for a waiver, which uses documents like letter 5597 or a certificate of discharge. Here is the secret sauce. If the IRS looks at the math and decides there isn't enough equity for them to actually make a profit flipping the house, meaning their right of redemption is basically valueless, they will issue you a release of that right completely for free. Now, if they do decide to take it, they'll file a certificate of redemption, pay you your formula amount, and the title legally transfers back to the United States. So, navigating federal tax redemption isn't about avoiding distressed property altogether. It's just about going in with your eyes wide open. You've got to know the timelines, you have to restrain yourself from starting those cosmetic flips too early, and you have to understand exactly how to work the system to clear your title safely, which leaves us with one final thought. In the high-stakes, fast-moving world of distressed real estate, are you strategic and patient enough to beat the IRS at their own game? Thanks for joining me on this explainer, and I'll catch you next time.

metadata.author: Logan Allec
metadata.shortDescription:
Owe the IRS or your state at least $10,000 in back taxes, or need to file multiple years of returns? Book a FREE consultation with Choice Tax Relief: call 866-8000-TAX or use the link below.
https://choicetaxrelief.com/free-tax-relief-consultation/?utm_source=YouTube&utm_medium=video_description&utm_campaign=youtube_organic&utm_content=joIEfxnWZzE&source_account=logan_allec

A federal tax lien is a legal claim against property. A Notice of Federal Tax Lien makes that claim public; a levy takes property. Logan Allec, CPA, explains Letter 3172, hearing rights, and four different approaches: release, discharge, subordination and withdrawal. letter you can ignore? It's not. A tax

works against you. A federal tax lien is
a public record that the IRS has a legal
claim to your property. That claim
attaches to your house, your car, your
bank accounts, and any future assets you
acquire while the lien is in place. It
damages your credit, often dropping your
score 100 points. It appears on
background checks for employment and
professional licenses. And a lien is

every paycheck until the debt is

Richard ignored his lien notice because

taking $59,000
and began garnishing 30% of his wages.

control of his entire financial life. Do
not let that happen. The moment you

happen more often than you would think.

owe. Check the tax years listed. Verify
that no payments or prior resolutions
have been credited incorrectly. The IRS
sometimes files liens for debts already
partially satisfied in or even belonging

your financial situation honestly. What
do you owe? What is your income? What
assets are at risk? This determines
which resolution option applies. Do not
guess. Get the facts in writing. Step

monthly payments, the IRS may agree to a

withdrawn. Miss one payment and the
agreement can collapse. Path three, an
offer in compromise. If you cannot pay
the full amount now or in the future,
you may qualify to settle for less.

accepted. You must prove inability to
pay with detailed financial disclosure.
An improperly filed OIC wastes time
while the lien remains. Path four,
currently not collectible status. If
your income barely covers living
expenses, you can request CNC.
Collection activity pauses, but this is
temporary. The IRS reviews your finances
periodically and the lien stays in
place. Choosing the wrong path costs you
time and leverage. A tax attorney
analyzes your numbers and recommends
what actually works, not what sounds
best on a commercial. If a lien has been
filed against you, do not navigate this
alone. Call 855-910-40
or you exactly where you stand. Step
four, get a tax attorney involved. This

attorney can negotiate lien
subordination, allowing you to sell or
refinance property with a lien in place.

filed lien through a collection due
process hearing. A tax attorney can
negotiate a lien withdrawal after you
enter a payment agreement, removing the

Our client, Laura, had a $400,000
federal tax lien blocking the sale of
her home. We negotiated a discharge of
the property from the lien so the sale
could proceed. Laura sold her home, paid

legal negotiation with the IRS Office of

Please feel free to check out our article, where we've written step by step instructions to help you walk through this tax form!  https://www.teachmepersonalfinance.com/irs-form-12277-instructions/

If you’re looking for tutorials for other IRS Forms that you can file directly through the IRS website, check out our free fillable forms page:  https://www.teachmepersonalfinance.com/free-fillable-tax-forms/

-If you currently have a federal tax lien, you may have some options, depending on your circumstances.

A "withdrawal" removes the public Notice of Federal Tax Lien and assures that the IRS is not competing with other creditors for your property; however, you are still liable for the amount due. 

One option may allow withdrawal of your Notice of Federal Tax Lien after the lien’s release. General eligibility includes:

Your tax liability has been satisfied and your lien has been released; and also:

-You are in compliance for the past three years in filing - all individual returns, business returns, and information returns;
-You are current on your estimated tax payments and federal tax deposits, as applicable.

The other option may allow withdrawal of your Notice of Federal Tax Lien if you have entered in or converted your regular installment agreement to a Direct Debit installment agreement. General eligibility includes:

-You are a qualifying taxpayer (i.e. individuals, businesses with income tax liability only, and out of business entities with any type of tax debt)
-You owe $25,000 or less (If you owe more than $25,000, you may pay down the balance to $25,000 prior to requesting withdrawal of the Notice of Federal Tax Lien)
-Your Direct Debit Installment Agreement must full pay the amount you owe within 60 months or before the Collection Statute expires, whichever is earlier
-You are in full compliance with other filing and payment requirements
-You have made three consecutive direct debit payments
-You can’t have defaulted on your current, or any previous, Direct Debit Installment agreement.

metadata.title: IRS Notice of Federal Tax Lien? DO NOT Skip the 30-Day Hearing
metadata.author: Read The Corner
metadata.shortDescription:
This video walks through the IRS collection letters in the order they usually arrive: CP14, CP501, CP503, the CP504 Notice of Intent to Levy, the Form 668(Y)(c) Notice of Federal Tax Lien, Letter 3172, LT11/Letter 1058, and the bank and wage levies (Forms 668-A and 668-W). It explains why Letter 3172 matters most: it gives you 30 days to file Form 12153 and request a Collection Due Process hearing. If you mail that form on day 31, you can usually only get an equivalent hearing, and you lose the right to take the decision to Tax Court.

0:23 The Anchor Numbers
1:00 The Pile
1:39 CP14 · The First Bill
2:22 CP501 · The Polite Nudge
3:03 CP503 · The Second Nudge

Pay in full by that date, and interest stops there. After that date, interest keeps accruing on what's left. A penalty runs alongside it. It is 0.5% of the unpaid tax, per month. It can climb to 25%. Slow, but it never takes a day off. Annoying, not scary. It is a bill, not a verdict. The fix: pay by the date inside, or ask for a plan. Next comes the CP501. It is a reminder. Same balance, slightly older. It is not a threat yet. It is a calendar reminder with a balance attached. Read one sentence twice. If you don't respond, they may file a lien. That sentence is the whole letter. Here is the calm part. You can apply online for a long-term plan. That works if you owe $50,000 or less. Online, with direct debit, setup is $29. And the monthly penalty drops to 0.25% on an approved plan. That's for individuals who filed on time. The fix: answer this one, even if only to start a plan. Then the CP503. The second reminder. The fix: pick the $29 door before the next envelope. Time for a case file. A composite, based on documented patterns. She gets a CP14 and puts it in a kitchen drawer. The CP501 and CP503 join it, unopened. Then a thicker envelope arrives, and the drawer won't close. The drawer kept every letter. It answered none of them. Which brings us to the CP504. This is the Notice of Intent to Levy. Levy means taking, not just claiming. This one deserves the whole desk. Read it twice, slowly, pencil in hand. It names wages and bank accounts. State tax refunds, too. And Social Security benefits. The law sets two timers here. First, 10 days after notice and demand to pay. Second, this written notice at least 30 days before a levy. Now the penalty changes gear. Miss 10 days after this notice, and it's 1% a month. Double the old rate. The fix: find the date, then call the number on the letter. A margin note from the desk. The mug would like to hold the CP504 flat. Denied. The corner stays dry. Then the lien itself: Form 668(Y)(c). This is the Notice of Federal Tax Lien being filed. A lien is a claim. Nothing has been taken yet. It is the paper this video is named after. It is public, which is the annoying part. But it is not the paper that matters most. It has an exit, and a side door. The exit: pay in full. The lien is released within 30 days after that. The side door is called withdrawal. Owe $25,000 or less. Be on a Direct Debit installment agreement. Make 3 consecutive direct debit payments. The debt must be paid within 60 months. Or before the collection deadline. Then ask, using Form 12277. Withdrawal means the public notice is taken back. The fix: get on direct debit early, then ask for withdrawal. Right behind the lien comes Letter 3172. This is the written notice owed within 5 business days.
