segments.text: So you found a federal tax lien attached to your house.
Maybe a title search turned it up, maybe an envelope showed up and you're staring
at it.
Either way, first question people ask is - is this normal? Am I being singled out?
You're not.
IRS Data Book numbers put Notice of Federal Tax Lien filings at 214,099 in FY2025.
Right. Up from 196,996 in FY2024, and 179,019 in FY2023.
So that's 8.7% in one year and 19.6% over two.
Okay, hold on. Because I keep hearing the IRS is falling apart.
Lost something like a quarter of its staff -
Roughly 27% of its workforce in 2025, yeah. And filings went up anyway.
That's the thing people get wrong.
A lien filing isn't a person pulling your file off a shelf and deciding you're the
problem.
It's automated. It's tied to your account balance.
So fewer humans to answer the phone doesn't slow down the system that generates
liens.
Hm. So the machine keeps going.
The machine keeps going.
What triggers it, though? Is there a number?
There's a guideline.
The IRS generally considers filing once your unpaid balance passes $10,000.
That threshold came out of the Fresh Start initiative.
But it's a guideline, not a wall - it can file under $10,000 if there's a pattern
of non-compliance, and it can hold off above $10,000 if you've already got a direct
debit installment agreement running.
And to be clear, not everybody who owes gets one.
No. 214,099 is a minority of delinquent accounts. It's discretionary.
Generally the larger or older balances.
Okay. Now the part that scared me reading this. The credit report thing.
Yeah, so the three major bureaus stopped listing tax liens on consumer credit
reports back in 2018.
Your FICO score doesn't move. Which sounds like good news and then it isn't.
Because -
Because it's still a public record.
Lenders, title companies, business creditors - they pull public records as a matter
of course.
So your score looks clean and your refinance still dies at the title search.
That's the one that blindsides homeowners.
Right, that's the part people miss. Okay. There's a clock in here somewhere.
Walk me through it.
Letter 3172.
That's the notice mailed after the lien is filed, and it starts a 30-day window to
request a Collection Due Process hearing on Form 12153.
Letter 3172, Form 12153. Thirty days from -
From the date on the letter. Find that date. Count it out.
That's the single most important number on the page, because the CDP hearing is the
strongest and cheapest way to challenge the lien or negotiate before things
escalate.
Miss it and that door closes.
And meanwhile interest and the late-payment penalty are still running.
The whole time. Every month.
Say more about where the lien sits in the sequence.
Because I don't think people realize this comes after a bunch of other mail.
It does. CP14 is the first balance-due bill, roughly 21 days.
Then CP501 and CP503, the reminders.
Then CP504 - that's intent to levy your state refund, and honestly that's usually
the last calm warning before a lien enters the picture.
Then Letter 3172, the lien.
Then separately, LT11 or Letter 1058, the final notice of intent to levy, with its
own 30 days before wage or bank levy.
Wait - two separate 30-day clocks?
Two separate events, two separate clocks.
People blend them together and lose one of them.
And the distinction underneath it all is simple: a lien secures the debt, a levy
takes your money.
On the transcript, is there a code?
Code 582 for the lien filed. A later release shows as code 583.
582 filed, 583 released. Okay. So a lien's on the property.
What are the actual moves?
Four buckets. Paying in full triggers a Certificate of Release within 30 days.
A withdrawal, that's Form 12277, actually erases the public notice - and that's
available if you paid in full, or if you owe $25,000 or less and you're making
direct debit installment payments.
Subordination is Form 14134, which lets a new lender take priority ahead of the IRS.
And discharge is Form 14135, which removes the lien from one specific property.
So withdrawal and subordination are the homeowner ones.
Those are the workhorses. Withdrawal if you want the record gone.
Subordination if you need to close on a refinance and you can't wait.
The article runs a hypothetical - the $13,600 one. Do that one for me.
Sure, and it is hypothetical.
Say you owe $13,600, balance crossed $10,000, lien got filed. You want to refinance.
Path one: you enter a streamlined direct debit installment agreement.
On a 72-month term that's roughly $189 a month before interest and before the
reduced 0.25% monthly late-payment penalty that applies while a plan's active.
And because you're under $25,000 on direct debit -
You become eligible to request the withdrawal on Form 12277 after some on-time
payments.
Path two, if the closing date won't wait, you file Form 14134 and ask the IRS to
subordinate.
The IRS often agrees when the refinance improves its position - cash-out proceeds
paying down the tax debt, for example.
Often agrees, not will agree.
Correct. The IRS runs its own math on every single request.
What you control is the paperwork, the timing, and whether you're compliant and in
a plan.
Not the answer.
Say the hard part out loud.
The hard part is sequence.
If a closing date is on the calendar, the order you do things in matters, and a
subordination request that goes in late or framed badly can blow the closing.
Same with a levy already in motion, unfiled years, payroll or business tax.
That's where it stops being a form-filling exercise.
And when is it genuinely DIY?
Clean and small.
Under $25,000, you can pay it off or you're on direct debit, you just want the
public record gone - Form 12277 is a reasonable do-it-yourself job.
Same with paying in full and confirming the Certificate of Release actually posted
with your county recorder.
Confirm it posted. Don't assume.
Don't assume. Nobody calls you to tell you the county record cleared.
One more - liens expire?
Tied to the ten-year collection statute, the CSED, which starts when the tax is
assessed.
Lien self-releases when that runs out. But tolling is the catch.
An Offer in Compromise, a CDP appeal, a bankruptcy filing - those pause the clock
and push the date out.
So it's rarely a clean ten calendar years.
Bankruptcy's not something you all handle, right?
That sits outside what Clarity does.
If it's on your mind, talk to your own counsel about it.
What we can do is Enrolled Agent work on the IRS side - transcripts, the lien
relief request, the payment arrangement.
Okay, next 24 hours. Give me three things.
One, find the date on your Letter 3172 and count thirty days.
Two, pull your account transcript and check the lien year and amount against your
own records - some liens get filed on balances that were already paid or misapplied.
Three, put your hands on your last filed return and a rough income-and-asset
snapshot.
And if there's a closing date.
Say it out loud when you call. 888-825-7779, free review.
The date on the calendar is what decides which relief actually fits.

metadata.title: How to Withdraw an IRS Tax Lien When You Owe $25,000 or Less
metadata.author: Bob Jablonsky
metadata.shortDescription:
Has the IRS filed a Notice of Federal Tax Lien against you? If your total assessed IRS balance is $25,000 or less, you may qualify to have the lien notice withdrawn while continuing to pay your tax debt through a Direct Debit Installment Agreement.

In this video, Bob Jablonsky, Enrolled Agent and Certified Tax Resolution Specialist, explains:

*  The difference between an IRS lien release and lien withdrawal
*  The IRS $25,000 lien-withdrawal threshold
*  Direct Debit Installment Agreement requirements
*  The three-consecutive-payment rule
*  Tax filing and payment compliance requirements
*  How to request withdrawal using IRS Form 12277
*  What happens to the underlying tax debt after withdrawal

Withdrawing the Notice of Federal Tax Lien removes the public notice, but it does not cancel the underlying IRS debt. You must continue making your monthly payments and remain compliant with all future tax obligations.

The applicable requirements are summarized on the IRS’s Understanding a federal tax lien page and in Form 12277.

Need help resolving an IRS tax lien or establishing the right payment plan? Contact Bob Jablonsky and Associates to discuss your situation.
https://jablonskytaxrelief.com/tax-relief-consultation/#books 

This video provides general educational information and is not individualized tax or legal advice.

metadata.title: IRS Redemption at Foreclosure - What will they refund me on?
metadata.author: LCO Law LLC | Estate Planning & Real Estate Law
metadata.shortDescription:
One of the risks of bidding at mortgage foreclosure or tax deed auctions in the State of Florida is that the IRS has the opportunity to redeem the property from you. While many investors are aware of the hundred and twenty day redemption period, few have clarity on what you can receive as a refund from the IRS and the time in which you have to claim that refund. The purpose of this video is to assist you in having a better understanding of what the IRS can refund you for, what it cannot refund you for, and how quickly you MUST act.

Natalia@lcolawfl.com
813-842-6664, 813-480-2106

Welcome to The Road to Financial Freedom, CamaPlan’s Premiere Podcast! In each episode, you will learn from successful self-directed investors and the people creating wealth-generating investment opportunities for them. Hear their stories, strategies, tactics, and life lessons that shaped their success to build the knowledge you need to achieve financial freedom.  In our profile and how-to series, guests share incredible stories and strategies that include Self-Directed IRAs, Roth IRAs, real estate, notes, investor hospitality, hard money loans, family investing, multi-family, self-storage, investment funds, Fair Market Values, asset protection, funding purchases, mineral and land rights, and tax liens. 

Episode Details:  In our quest for a diversified portfolio, we may get tripped up on knowing where to turn next. Where can you expand your expertise and venture into new investments that will help you grow your wealth, and how do earn those desired high returns on investments without running the high risk? This is what Joanne Musa, famously known as the Tax Lien Lady, has been educating thousands of investors on when it comes to investing in tax liens and tax deeds. As the number one trusted expert in the United States on the matter, Joanne has been a major contributor to real estate investing websites and to several best-selling publications on Amazon. Listen to her personal journey to hear how she found this type of investing and expand your education on the benefits of tax lien investing.

metadata.title: 🏠 Tax Deed Challenge: Defective Notice, Rushed Auction & Summary Judgment Without Evidence
metadata.author: Florida Trust, Real Estate, Probate, & Foreclosure
metadata.shortDescription:
Betty Horne v. Miami-Dade County, Florida, etc., et al. | Case No. 3D11-1806 | Florida Third District Court of Appeal

A homeowner sought to vacate a tax deed on her longtime residence, and the tax-deed purchaser, Metropolitan Homes, sued to quiet title. The consolidated cases ended in summary judgment for the purchaser, county, and clerk. Counsel for the homeowner argues that the notice of application for tax deed omitted her name as trustee, contrary to the statute and the Department of Revenue form, that she had no actual notice, and that the auction closed so quickly a bidder was cut off. The panel presses the appellees on where the record contains any properly authenticated summary judgment evidence of notice, and on what additional steps the clerk took after certified mail came back, as Jones v. Flowers and Delta Property Management require. Counsel for the county and clerk acknowledges the record is thin and that they had moved to relinquish jurisdiction for fact-finding. The panel also questions how a resale could put the purchaser back in its pre-sale position.

KEY ISSUES:
• Does a notice of application for tax deed that omits an owner's name defeat the tax deed?
• Does the tax deed's prima facie presumption of regularity under § 197.552 excuse the lack of summary judgment evidence?
• What additional reasonable steps must the clerk take when certified-mail notice is returned?
• Can a certificate of mailing attached to a complaint serve as summary judgment evidence without a business-records predicate?
• Was a rushed close of the tax-deed auction a genuine issue of material fact?
• Can the trial court resolve disputed facts by reviewing an auction video in camera on summary judgment?

LEGAL AUTHORITY:
• Jones v. Flowers, 547 U.S. 220 (2006) — additional steps after returned notice
• Delta Property Management, Inc. v. Profile Investments, Inc., 87 So. 3d 765 (Fla. 2012) — clerk's duty after failed tax-deed notice
• Wells v. Thomas (Fla. 1956) (as quoted by counsel at argument) — defective notice of tax-deed application

RULES & STATUTES DISCUSSED:
• Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.510 — summary judgment: https://www.floridarules.net/civil-procedure/#rule-1-510
• §§ 197.402, 197.512, 197.542, 197.552, Fla. Stat. — tax-deed notice, sale, and presumption of regularity
• § 65.081, Fla. Stat. — quiet title by tax-deed grantee

🔗 Florida Rules & Legal Resources: https://www.floridarules.net

#TaxDeed #PropertyTax #QuietTitle #DueProcess #SummaryJudgment #TaxDeedSale #Foreclosure #RealEstateLaw #ThirdDCA #FloridaAppeal

metadata.title: Jones v. SEC — 5th Cir. (Nov 2, 2026)
metadata.author: Oral Arguments, with Context
metadata.shortDescription:
The Fifth Circuit hears Robbi Jones and Kipling Jones and Company's challenge to sanctions upheld by the Securities and Exchange Commission. The dispute began with a certificate of deposit pledged as loan collateral but counted toward the firm's required net capital. FINRA, the securities industry's self-regulatory organization, found that this overstated the firm's financial cushion and produced inaccurate records and reports. It also found that Jones gave misleading answers and failed to cooperate fully with its investigation. On FINRA appeal, a two-year suspension was increased to a bar from associating with FINRA member firms in any capacity. The SEC later upheld the violations and sanctions after a review that took years. Jones and her firm now argue that the penalty was excessive and that the process was constitutionally defective. Their lawyer will argue that FINRA functions as a government enforcer, even though it is organized as a private body. He will question whether SEC oversight provided meaningful protection while the bar was already in effect. The government's lawyer will argue that the SEC's rulemaking, review, and stay powers keep FINRA subordinate to a federal agency. The lawyer for FINRA will defend its private status and argue that key objections were not raised at earlier stages of the case. A threshold issue is whether particular objections were raised in time. Those procedural questions are distinct from whether the bar is too severe or the regulator's powers are constitutional.

Jones v. SEC (No. 25-60703) — U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, argued November 2, 2026.

https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/OralArgRecordings/25/25-60703_11-02-2026.mp3

Case and argument date — official Fifth Circuit recording archive:
https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/oral-argument-recordings/results?from=2026-08-01&to=2026-11-05&page=2

Financial reporting, investigation, sanctions and prior SEC review — SEC Release 104273, November 28, 2025, File 3-20209; not this appeal's outcome:
https://www.sec.gov/files/litigation/opinions/2025/34-104273.pdf

videos.full_text: In this episode, the Fifth Circuit hears Robbie Jones and Kipling Jones and company's challenge to sanctions upheld by the Securities and Exchange Commission. The dispute began with a certificate of deposit pledged as loan collateral, but counted toward the firm's required net capital. FINRA, the securities industry's self-regulatory organization, found that this overstated the firm's financial cushion and produced inaccurate records and reports. It also found that Jones gave misleading answers and failed to cooperate fully with its investigation. On FINRA appeal, a two-year suspension was increased to a bar from associating with FINRA member firms in any capacity. The SEC later upheld the violations and sanctions after a review that took years. Jones and her firm now argue that the penalty was excessive and that the process was constitutionally defective. Their lawyer will argue that FINRA functions as a government enforcer, even though it is organized as a private body. He will question whether SEC oversight provided meaningful protection while the bar was already in effect. The government's lawyer will argue that the SEC's rule making, review, and stay powers keep FINRA subordinate to a federal agency. The lawyer for FINRA will defend its private status and argue that key objections were not raised at earlier stages of the case. A threshold issue is whether particular objections were raised in time. Those procedural questions are distinct from whether the bar is too severe or the regulator's powers are constitutional. >> Good Your Honors, and may it please the court. My name is Matthew Hoxie, and along with my colleague, Mr. Dominic Dray, we represent petitioners Robert Jones and Kipling Jones and Company. Ms. Jones is in the courtroom today and greatly appreciates the court's attention to this matter. I'll try to reserve reserve 5 minutes of my time for rebuttal. This case concerns the SEC's doppelganger, FINRA, and the manner in which it enforces and adjudicates cases involving the securities laws of the United States, including FINRA rules, which once adopted by the SEC, carry the force of law. In this case, those processes led to an excessive and oppressive sanction and violated the Constitution in three principal ways. As a state actor, FINRA was required to provide due process, jury trial under the 7th Amendment, and comport with the Appointments Clause. It did neither. To the extent FINRA possesses broad regulatory immunity when it stands in the shoes of the SEC and enforces and adjudicates federal securities law, so too must it honor the Constitution's protections. To hold otherwise would be to allow the government, in contravention of the warning of the Lebron court, to evade its most solemn obligations by resort to a corporate form. As a threshold matter, petitioners do not rely solely on the argument that FINRA is a part of the government in every capacity in order to succeed today. It would be sufficient for our purposes for this court to hold that FINRA's enforcement and adjudicatory actions are state action that require constitutional compliance. But petitioners do believe that FINRA is part of the government. The government's argument otherwise is based on a broad overreading of the Lebron decision, which they argue established three sole and exclusive factors for determining whether an entity is part of the government. That is that it is created by the government for furtherance of government objective, with the government retaining authority to appoint a majority of the board. The principal case the Lebron court relies on would have failed the first factor right out of the gate. That is Pennsylvania, the board of directors of City Trust of Philadelphia, in which the US Supreme Court held that Girard College, which was established pursuant to a private trust, so not created by the government, was nevertheless part of the government because it was operated and maintained by a state trustee. What the Lebron court said was that if that was part of the government, then Amtrak represented a quote a fortiori case. We think that's a proper way to look at it. There are a variety of circumstances that might render an entity part of the government, just as Girard College was. So too was Amtrak and Amtrak probably represents excuse me, far into the spectrum easy case. Um if the court is inclined to look for how this current US Supreme Court would consider the matter, it need look no further than then Judge Gorsuch's decision. >> Can I ask you, I mean, I know that she didn't want the two years, but then it turned into life. Have they ever explained why it went from two years to life? >> Uh your honors, no from our view and we frankly find it concerning. When we looked at a or similar cases, particularly the Mary Mack case, I'll point your honors to page 58 of the government's brief because I think it provides the justification in this case. There in the case of Mary Mack, there was a $225,000 fine imposed and one year suspension for falsifying and forging records. That's far worse conduct than my client was found to be in violation of. The government's excuse for why that was appropriate is because the party didn't appeal. I think that's a warning shot to any industry participant that if you challenge FINRA and do not simply pay its initial fine or accept your initial punishment, they will increase the sanction for merely exercising your right to appeal. I think that's the only justification that I can read from the briefing in this case, your honor. And what FINRA has done here, and this distinguishes this from other cases that might involve simple private club rules, is to enforce uh and find a violation of federal securities law. I think this case can be resolved with they answering a few basic questions. Did FINRA find a violation and enforce federal securities law? Yes, that was Exchange Act Rule 17A3 and A5. Did FINRA disbar my client? Yes. Did that bar take immediate effect without an automatic stay pending an appeal? Yes, and that places this case on all fours with the majority decision in Alpine Securities. Um the district court or the circuit court decision in that case noted that the ability to file a motion for a stay did not absolve the constitutional infirmities. Uh the SEC in denying my client's stay request in this case, that was denied in February 2021, noted the same standard. It requires an extraordinary remedy. And in fact, in that denial decision, noted that financial harm suffered in the meantime did not rise to the level of irreparable injury warranting a stay. We know from the the facts in this case, the SEC's review does not come until 4 and 1/2 years after the completion of briefing. I also think the SEC probably placed themselves in a position where they had to affirm a lifetime bar because to hold otherwise would have resulted in them affirming, for example, a 2-year sanction, but my client suffering being barred for 5 years. Um so again, I think the >> Well, but that's why I was wondering why they didn't Oh, sorry. Why they just didn't do 5 years or whatever? I mean, some other number other than life. >> That's a question I think better served for my friends on the other side. We believe there's no justification for it, particularly looking at like cases. Um again, the other case that we pointed to and the parties have litigated over is David Allen Elgert. There is similarly there were was uh a false statement provided to FINRA and the intentional filing of false reports. Um the government >> we get to all of that, I don't think you've discussed any waiver or forfeiture arguments at all. And I think a lot of the arguments from the other side are going to say that you've um you've forfeited the Seventh Amendment claims and you've forfeited several other claims for for failing to argue them or brief them correctly or to fail to present them before FINRA. Is that correct? >> That is correct, Your Honor. Those are the SEC and FINRA's arguments. The argument that we failed to present them to the issues to FINRA itself is made only by FINRA. It's not made by the SEC as an argument here for waiver. I would note that the primary case upon which FINRA relies is called Merrill Lynch things from 1980, long predates Axon, Enterprise Fund, a number of cases that have that have found the exhaustion requirements of 15 U.S.C. Section 78Y do not encompass constitutional claims. And I think the argument particularly in that regard, we can look to page 194 of the Axon decision for why constitutional claims such as the Seventh Amendment, which we acknowledge we did not raise to to FINRA or the SEC below, fall outside of it. And that is because the inquiry turns on the nature, not on the status pending or not in the agency proceeding. Just as well Seventh Amendment and constitutional claims lie outside of the agency's competency and expertise. That holds true regardless of the stage of an agency proceeding. Even if we hadn't raised those to as we didn't to the to the SEC, there was an intervening change of law. We've noted the Giuriceo case and futility. >> There There was some time after that decision came out, the Giuriceo decision came out before the final decision was issued. Is there a reason why those matters were not raised before after that time? >> There is, Your Honor. We believed it would have only been futile and led to additional delays. We understand that >> that alerting them of a U.S. Supreme Court decision was going to be futile? >> Yes, Your Honor. Well, we have a long and broken chain of the SEC taking the sole position that Seventh Amendment doesn't attach to FINRA proceedings. They've never pointed to a case and cannot point to a case to our knowledge where they have held otherwise, and I would also note the primary case in the government relies on a the Smith Sixth Circuit decision. The primary fact there, one of the factors the court looked to, was a similar case, Ricky Allen Mante, where the party was unable to file a motion to supplement the record effectively. That was granted in October 2024 in that case. Since then, the SEC has only continuously granted themselves further extensions to rule. If we hadn't briefed out the Jarkesy question, I doubt we would have had a SEC decision to this day. And so it's those delays which really undermine the government's arguments to sufficient SEC review of the adjudicatory function. In other cases, the SEC argues with respect to rule-making authority, what we're discussing here are principally enforcement, so an executive type function that begins with the launching of an investigation. That occurred years ago. Nevertheless, bears the burden or bears the weight of the government coming down on industry members because with FINRA, there is mandatory membership, just like there is with the PCAOB, mandatory membership. And there, there's no dispute, PCAOB is a part of the government for constitutional purposes. The enforcement followed through with an adjudication. That led to the 2020 NAC decision, and then we did not have an SEC review on the merits for several years. There was simply a lack of sufficient SEC review of FINRA investigations and adjudications. Particularly on the investigations, we think that's conceded by FINRA's brief recognizing and proposing a potential pre-clearance rule that does not exist and did not apply. The vast majority of FINRA investigations resolve via settlement. We've noted that in our our briefings citing Commissioner Pierce's firsthand observations. 90% or more of investigations resolve in settlement. And what's interesting about that is those settlements are entirely inoculated from SEC review. Under Exchange Act 15 USC 70 76 or 78 SE, the SEC can only statutorily review a final disciplinary sanction. A settlement, which takes the form under FINRA's proceedings as an acceptance waiver or consent, AWC, is not a final disciplinary sanction. So, FINRA in the vast majority of cases imposes its enforcement authority on parties, imposes fines, collects those fines, and reaches a settlement where party member or industry members pay those fines, all without any SEC review. And in fact, SEC cannot review those. The SEC has approved what's called FINRA Rule 9216. By signing a settlement, even if it lied outside of the SEC's Exchange Act authority to review a case, um FINRA Rule 9216 requires waiver of any appeal or challenge to a settlement. And those are, again, entirely inoculated from SEC review. That is the full bearing of weight of FINRA's actions. The government's argument in this case primarily relies on strict form over function. We see that with their attempt to distinguish PCAOB for Enterprise Fund, for example, by contending government creation as a mandatory factor. Again, we think that's not even in comporting with the primary case the Lebron court relied on. In function, though, and that's what matters is the function, PCAOB operates similarly and was set up to mirror the functions of SROs. Just to absolve this court of worry, the SRO that is FINRA is far differently situated than an SRO like Nasdaq, which was at issue in the Alliance for Fair Board Recruitment case. There you do have competing SRO exchanges. Those are different. They are fairly, I think, attributed to be regulated parties. FINRA is as tour space. Particularly, again when they enforce and adjudicate cases involving the securities law. Um for enforcement, we point the court to foot footnote nine in the National Enforcement case listing a litany of cases finding that the exercise of an investigation or enforcement powers equates to executive power. >> Uh didn't that case also um list a litany of reasons why the SEC was different from the agency in that case? >> Yes, Your Honor, it did. Uh to be fair, SEC was not actually at issue in that case and I think what the court was considering is the theoretical um limitations or oversight that the SEC purportedly has over FINRA. Those don't operate in practice. One of the reasons is uh or given in that case was that the SEC can purportedly derecognize FINRA. Um that's a hollow threat. Even Commissioner Peirce in the article we cite notes that FINRA is the only self-regulatory organization in that field. SEC could not step into the void that would be left. Um and I think it's particularly important to pay attention to the size of FINRA in that regard. FINRA's budget is 1.5 approximately billion dollars. That near mirrors the SEC. That is five times higher nearly than the PCAOB. It's higher than the FTC, FCC, and a litany of agencies. If FINRA were properly considered part of the government, it would immediately become one of the largest by budget. Um and we think the best possible cases for this court to look to if it is not sold with us on the part of the government test argument, but viewing this as sufficient for state actor purposes, the enforcement and adjudicatory powers. Brentwood Academy, there where you had the Tennessee Board of Education approve the private interscholastic organization's rules and back through enforcement um the enforcement of that against members. We'd also point the court to Marsh v. Alabama, a company town that was indistinguishable from any other town. FINRA is indistinguishable from its patron agency. Uh and then finally, we'd point the court to Terry v. Adams, duplication of a government uh function. The government wants to argue in this case that the government function is regulating securities market. That's only half true. The function here is really again enforcement and adjudication of federal law. That lies within the purview of the government. Uh unless there's any further questions, I'll reserve the remaining of my time for rebuttal. >> Good afternoon, Your Honors. May it please the court. Steven Hazel for the government. I want to start by clarifying how the different constitutional doctrines in this case fit together. In Horsman, this court said an entity is either governmental for constitutional purposes or it's not. And the way to make that determination is the test in Lebron. For all the same reasons that the entity, the private entity in Horsman's, was not governmental, neither is FINRA. Um this court in Horsman's went on to say Lebron is the test, it's the only test, you can't add to it. We can't bypass that Supreme Court decision. That's why uh petitioners making references to these state action decisions just are not relevant under Horsman. So, because FINRA is not governmental, then the question becomes one of private non-delegation. Um and as this court uh recognized uh in Horsman, uh this is a situation where Congress has made clear that the buck stops with SEC. Uh Congress has given SEC potent oversight powers, to use this court's language in Horsman. I would draw this court's attention to three features of this statute in particular. First, on the front end, uh SEC can change uh the rules, uh including the rules about how these disciplinary processes operate, when investigations are launched. Uh whenever it doesn't like what's happening, it can change the rules on the front end. Um on the back end, uh if SEC is unhappy about a particular uh violation or sanction, uh it can perform de novo review both of the finding of violation and of the sanction itself. It can also stay any any sanctions before they go into effect. And here I'll note petitioners did file a stay motion. I believe that SEC adjudicated the motion within a week and it decided that they hadn't raised a serious merits question. I think that underscores that the SEC is the one in control here. The fact that petitioners don't like the result of that stay motion and don't like the result of that stay order, that does not in any way suggest that SEC >> Why go from 2 years to life? >> So, Yoran, I think there were significant aggregate aggravating factors that SEC looked at here. Petitioner had already been put on heightened supervision. She'd been told that you couldn't have a pledge certificate of deposit as part of your net capital. She'd been told that like within a year before these additional violations. And then despite that warning, she she did it again and then she lied about having done that. She lied about the fact that it was pledged. And SEC views these net capital requirements as especially important because they go to whether a firm can serve their customers effectively. SEC in this order said it perceived a risk to customers and and investors and that goes a long way to explaining why when it performed this de novo review, it it upheld the sanction. I I just want to briefly make sure I've I've sort of covered the full range of SEC's statutory authority over FINRA here. The one other bucket that I would point this court to is something that Horsemen also emphasized, which is if SEC doesn't like how FINRA's enforcement is playing out, it can take away FINRA's enforcement authority altogether. It can even view recognize FINRA as one of these organizations and it can conduct its own enforcement. That's all part of why this court enforcement uh said that uh this situation is radically different than the situation that concerned the court there. Uh my friend on the other side um mentioned Alpine and said this case is on all all fours with Alpine. Uh I strongly disagree with that. Alpine was an as-applied challenge. Uh the DC Circuit was concerned about an immediate effect before SEC review. Uh that's nothing like this case. There has been SEC review. This is a challenge to an SEC uh order. Um so the logic of Alpine uh points squarely against petitioners here. Um indeed, this statutory scheme has been around since the 1930s and underpins the financial system and as the Sixth Circuit said not long ago, case after case has has upheld it. Uh we would urge this court to do the same. Uh petitioners uh also talked about settlement. Um Respectfully, there was no settlement here. I take them to be offering a facial challenge. Um if there were concerns about sort of how a particular settlement played out, uh this court could consider them in an as-applied case. I'd also note that uh as we were discussing a few minutes ago, uh as part of its ability to change the rules, uh SEC could, if it wanted, uh require pre-approval of settlements or impose other limitations on when FINRA in enters a settlement uh with with private parties. Uh so I don't think that gets them very far. Um I'm happy to answer any other questions this court has on non-delegation. Otherwise, I'll turn um briefly to to forfeiture. Um I Congress made clear that it wanted arguments uh to be raised before SEC if they were going to then be brought in court. Uh petitioners know that. Um before SEC, they raised a number of constitutional arguments. Uh they chose, for whatever reason, to admit their Seventh Amendment argument. That means they can't possibly have a reasonable basis for excusing the forfeiture. That's what the Sixth Circuit recognized unanimously in Smith just a few months ago. Uh they haven't found uh any basis for distinguishing this case. Uh I'll also note uh that this court has recognized similar statutory bars apply equally to constitutional claims. So we think that's >> And we couldn't apply it as a plain error? >> I don't think so, Your Honor. I I I don't believe they've they've even made any sort of plain error argument here. I think the the text of the statute Congress made made clear that that wasn't what it wanted courts to do when an argument is not raised before the SEC. I'm happy to answer any further questions the court may have. Otherwise, I'll see at the balance of my time. >> May it please the court, Allison Ho for intervener FINRA. Petitioners' constitutional claims against FINRA fail because they're all forfeited and meritless besides. The private non-delegation claim is a non-starter under the Supreme Court's decision in Consumers Research and this court's decision in Horsemen's 3, which used the FINRA-SEC relationship as the exemplar for compliance with the private non-delegation doctrine. The rest of petitioners' constitutional claims depend on treating FINRA like the federal government. But no court that's considered the question has ever held that FINRA is a state actor or engages in state action. Horsemen's 3 confirmed that Lebron is the governing state actor test and FINRA passes with flying colors because it's industry created, industry funded, and industry-staffed. So it's not a state actor. It doesn't fall into any of the narrow state action exceptions, either. Securities discipline was never an exclusively government function. That's the Supreme Court's decision in Jackson. Mere approval isn't compulsion. That's the Supreme Court's decision in Bloom. Brentwood entwinement is entirely absent. And heavy regulation doesn't create state action under Halek. The petition should be denied. There are no questions, Your Honor. So, I'm happy to cede back the rest of my time. >> Um, I do have one question. >> Yes, Your Honor. >> What I'm you you've cited to several sources um in the brief that you filed before the court. But, what's your best authority from um one of the article article three courts that fell you to assert a claim before FINRA FINRA constitutes forfeiture of the issue? >> Certainly. Um I think uh two cases I would point um one case is this court's decision um that we rely on in Merrill Lynch. Um there is also a a decision um it's out of circuit, but it's straight on point and that's the MFS decision at 380 F. 3rd at 622, which talks about the rationale for raising claims before FINRA in the first instance um primarily because objections should be made uh where the record is made as as well. That gives FINRA an opportunity um to uh build the record so that the SEC is then able uh to better review that record in the first instance, Your Honor. If that's responsive to your question. >> Thank you. >> And one more point um Your Honor on Judge Douglas on your questions with respect to uh the statutory exhaustion bar in 78 YC1. Um contrary to my friend on the other side's position, there there is no there is no reasonable ground exception or excuse for constitutional claims. This court enforced the bar in Burford. The Sixth Circuit enforced the bar in a materially indistinguishable case in in Smith. So, even if the claim wasn't forfeited because it had not been raised for FINRA before FINRA, it would be independently and doubly forfeited because it was not raised before the SEC. That's the Seventh Amendment claim in particular, as my friend on the other side concedes, Your Honor. Thank you. >> She's [clears throat] excused. >> Oh, I'm sorry. Yes. >> Thank you, Your Honor. >> Your Honors, if you are looking for any indication how the current US Supreme Court would handle the Lebron analysis in the government's argument, the court need look no further than then Judge Gorsuch's decision on the 10th Circuit, case called United States v. Ackerman, that's cited in Judge Walker's concurrence in the Alpine Securities case. It's 831 F.3d 1292. Applying Lebron and post-Lebron, the 10th Circuit, with Judge then Judge Gorsuch writing, found that the private National Center for Missing Exploited Children was nevertheless part of the government. What matters, according to then Judge Gorsuch, is, quote, "What the entity does, not how it is organized." Tellingly absent from that case is any indication the government had authority, for example, to appoint a majority of the board. The court actually wrote only approximately a quarter or 25% of board members were government officials, and nevertheless, based on what the government did in that case or what the entity did in that case, it was part of the government. Um we think a straight forward application to FINRA and its enforcement and adjudication of federal securities law would reach the same result. The SEC argues they can always change the rules. That only shows an abdicate abdication of authority in this space and an insufficient level of SEC review. Regarding the aggravating circumstances, we responded to that in our briefing. That's a misuse of aggravators is a clear due process error. Regarding non-delegation and Consumers Research, the government's argument principally relies on that case as well as Sunshine Anthracite. But what's important is this is exactly as the court in National Horseman's recognized, nothing the administrator with within the Consumers Research case did took any legal or practical effects without the government's say-so. metadata.title: Why Retirees Are Losing Paid-Off Homes Over $3,000 Tax Bills
metadata.author: The Quiet Math
metadata.shortDescription:
Across America, older homeowners are losing houses they paid off years ago — over property tax bills of a few thousand dollars, sometimes a few hundred. The house is free and clear; the tax bill is what takes it.

In this video, we follow one composite story, a retired machinist and widower, through the rule almost every new retiree misses: when your mortgage is paid off, the bank stops paying your property taxes. We break down how unpaid property taxes become a tax lien sold to an investor, how interest, the next years' taxes, fees and legal costs turn $3,000 into almost $14,000 during the redemption period, why certified letters and unanswered calls fail older homeowners, what the Supreme Court said in Jones v. Flowers (2006) and Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) about notice and home equity theft, and one question to ask your parents this week about senior property tax exemptions and freezes.

Harold, the person in this story, is a composite character built from patterns that repeat across many real cases. He is not one real individual.

📊 Sources
- Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023)
- Jones v. Flowers, 547 U.S. 220 (2006)
- The Washington Post, "Homes for the Taking" (2013), summarized by the Washingtonian
- National Consumer Law Center, "The Other Foreclosure Crisis: Property Tax Lien Sales" (2012)

If this story matters to you, subscribe — we break down where the numbers quietly stopped working for ordinary people.

This video is for informational and educational purposes only and is not financial advice or legal advice. Property tax, tax lien and redemption rules vary by state — check with your county treasurer or a local legal aid office.

#PropertyTax #AmericanRetirees #housingcrisis

segments.text: There's a sheet of paper taped to the front
door, white letter size held flat with
clear packing tape at all four corners
so the wind can't take it.
A 77-year-old man stands on his own porch
and reads it through his bifocals.
Twice.
It has his address on it,
a date, and a word he has only ever seen
in the back pages of the newspaper.
Foreclosure.
This is the story of how a man can lose
a house he finished paying for 14 years
ago over a property tax bill of about $3,000.
But the $3,000 is not really what came
for his house.
Something quieter did.
We'll get to it.
Stories like this sound too small to be
real.
They are not rare.
In 2013, a Washington Post investigation
went through every tax lien sold on homes
in the nation's capital since 2005.
The reporters found homeowners who had
lost their houses over debts of a few hundred
dollars.
Some owed less than a hundred.
Several of them were elderly.
Many of them own their homes outright.
The man on the porch is Harold.
He's not one real person.
He's a composite built from patterns that
show up again and again in these stories.
And from the court records those stories
leave behind.
Harold ran a lathe for 36 years at a plant
that made valve parts in an old factory
city in the Northeast.
Second shift mostly.
He came home smelling of cutting oil and
his wife, June, kept the books.
Every bill, every checkbook,
every envelope with a little plastic window
went across her side of the kitchen table.
For 46 years, that was the deal.
They bought a narrow brick house for $31,000
When Harold was 63, they made the last
payment.
The bank mailed a letter to confirm it
and June put that letter in a frame and
hung it in the hallway next to their wedding
picture.
Harold rebuilt the porch steps himself
the following summer.
He likes to say the house has never once
let him down.
In our last story, we met Marlene,
a retired housekeeper who lost her lease
and ended up paying for a motel room by
the week.
Harold's story was supposed to be the opposite.
No landlord, no lease to renew,
no rent to raise.
The house is worth about $210,000 and every
brick of it is his.
On paper, he was the safe one.
His social security is about $2,100 a month.
There's a small pension from the plant,
$340, and it hasn't gone up once since
the day he retired.
With no mortgage, that was enough.
The property tax ran about $2,880 a year
in two bills, one in the spring and one
in the fall.
June paid both the week they came.

In this video, we'll provide you with information about tax lien sales in Illinois. We'll explain what a tax lien is and how it works, and we'll share some resources with you that you can use to find out more about Illinois tax liens. https://tedthomas.com/ytl-27100/

Video Highlights:
🏦 Tax lien sales in Illinois involve the auctioning of delinquent properties by the treasurer.
📅 The auctions typically take place during the summer months, and each county has its own schedule.
🏠 Property owners have up to 30 months to redeem the tax lien by paying the back taxes and interest.
🤝 Any member of the public can participate in the auction, but registration and financial qualifications are required.
💰 The interest rates offered on tax liens are determined through a bid-down process, with the lowest rate winning the certificate.

metadata.title: How to Buy County-Held Tax Liens on LienHub (Florida Example)
metadata.author: The Jackie Jackson | Tax Deed & Real Estate Coach
metadata.shortDescription:
County-held tax liens are tax lien certificates that didn't sell at the county's annual sale, and in Florida you can buy them from the county after the sale. In this 2020 video, I walk through LienHub, a website some Florida counties use for their tax certificate sales and county-held certificates, and show how I searched Lake County, Florida's county-held certificates there, then checked one property on the county tax collector's and property appraiser's websites.

When I recorded this, registering on LienHub was free, and you could look at the county list without logging in. I show you where the county-held list is, how to filter it by tax year and usage code, and how to download it to a spreadsheet so you can sort it your way.

Buying a tax lien doesn't excuse you from doing your due diligence. For the certificate I clicked on, I check whether taxes for other years are unpaid, the property's usage code (this one is vacant residential land), the zoning, the flood map, and the frontage and depth. The aerial view showed what looked like a retention pond, and the lot measurements made me wonder if it was even buildable. That's what you want to find out before you buy. You buy a county-held certificate for the interest, so you want a property the owner is likely to redeem.

In Florida, a certificate nobody buys at the annual sale is struck to the county at the maximum rate (18% a year), and anyone can buy it from the county before a tax deed application is made. You only collect that interest if the owner pays the taxes back. If the owner doesn't, Florida has a process to enforce it: after a waiting period, the certificate holder can file a tax deed application with the tax collector, the owner is notified, and the property can go to a tax deed sale. It doesn't promise you'll get your money back, so read the law first. Florida's is Chapter 197 of the Florida Statutes, and every state has its own.

metadata.author: Personal Finance Tips
metadata.shortDescription:
This week, I deep dive on tax lien investing with Phil Kessler, a prolific tax lien investor who has extensively researched the tax lien investing laws of multiple states. He also creates a lot of educational content about tax lien and tax deed investing online.

Investing in tax liens may sound scary and complicated. But as you’ll see from today’s podcast interview, with a little bit of research upfront, it can be as easy as buying toilet paper on Amazon. And the capital required to invest can be as little as a couple hundred bucks, making it a low-risk way (compared to buy-and-hold real estate) to try a new investing strategy.

We discuss:

- How tax lien investing works + how to make money from it
- Differences between tax lien vs. tax deed investing
- How tax lien interest rates are set + realistic rates you can expect
- What makes an ideal tax lien investment
- Due diligence checklist for analyzing tax lien deals (and how it differs from typical real estate investing due diligence)
- Tips and tricks for evaluating physical property condition, environmental risks, etc, when you can’t access the house
- How tax lien auctions work + winning bid strategies
- How tax lien investment funds work + tradeoffs of investing in a fund

Check it out here:

https://hackyourwealth.com/tax-lien-investing

Have you ever invested in tax liens? What’s been your experience? What other questions do you have about it? Let me know by leaving a comment.

P.S. If you liked this episode, be sure to subscribe on Apple Podcasts so you don’t miss any upcoming episodes! 😎

https://hackyourwealth.com/itunes

P.P.S. Join us on Facebook! 

https://hackyourwealth.com/fb

Unlock the power of passive income and secure your financial future with our video on Maximizing Returns: The Power of Investing in Tax Liens. This comprehensive video will guide you through the process of investing in tax liens, a often-overlooked but highly profitable investment strategy.

Tax liens are a legal claim placed on a property by a government entity for unpaid taxes. As an investor, you can purchase these liens at auction, and earn a return on your investment through interest and penalties on the delinquent taxes. In some cases, you may even have the opportunity to gain ownership of the property if the taxes remain unpaid.

This video will teach you the ins and outs of tax lien investing, including how to research and identify profitable tax lien opportunities, how to bid and win at tax lien auctions, and how to manage and collect on your investments. It also covers the benefits of tax lien investing, such as high returns, low risk, and the potential for long-term passive income.

Our experienced investment professionals will also share their tips and strategies for maximizing returns, and give you a better understanding of the potential for profitability in the tax lien market.

Whether you're a seasoned investor looking for a new opportunity, or a beginner looking for a secure and profitable investment strategy, Maximizing Returns: The Power of Investing in Tax Liens is the perfect video for you. Take control of your financial future and learn how to earn passive income with tax lien investing today.

Investing in Real Estate Tax Lien Certificates: Case Study - learn Real Estate Investing
What you will learn in this course ?
What you'll learnLearning the ins and outs of investing in Florida Tax Lien Certificates by way of a case study.The difference between a tax lien certificate and a tax deed.We will look at two of the main websites that host the auctions for the Florida tax lien certificate auctions (Grant Street and Real Auction).County-Held certificates are also an investment option where the counties will sell their certificates at an 18% interest rate.We will go over the tax deed application process if a property tax owner does not pay their tax liability within the redemption period.
This is an actual case study of my journey into investing in Florida tax lien certificates. I will use my own funds and invest in this asset class for the first time and share my experience with you. This course will look at the State of Florida only. Most of the counties in the state conduct their auctions online.  And each of these counties use a third-party to run conduct these auctions and to run the software on their websites. We will look at two of these companies that handle most of the counties within the state.Grant Street (LienHub) - for Hillsborough, Pinellas, Pasco and Dade (Miami)RealTaxLien (Real Auction) - for Sarasota and Polk CountyMy strategy for this investment is to not use the tax lien certificates as a way of owning real property.My goal is to find properties that will redeem quickly so I can earn a return on investment that is greater than the money earned by leaving it in a bank and is secured by real estate. Interest rates on tax lien certificates in the state of Florida start out at 18% and then get bid downwards in a reverse-style auction. We will also discuss tax deed applications and the auctions that arise from these applications after the redemption period has expired.  This is a way for the tax lien certificate holder to force a foreclosure sale. There are also county-held certificates that can be purchased at any time that accrue interest at an 18% annual return.  DISCLAIMERI am not an investment professional.  Please discuss any investment with the appropriate professionals to see if this would make sense for your personal situation.

metadata.title: Where Are Tax Deed Auctions Held? How I Find Online County Sales
metadata.author: The Jackie Jackson | Tax Deed & Real Estate Coach
metadata.shortDescription:
Tax deed auctions are usually held at the county level, and some counties hold them online while others hold them in person, like at the clerk of courts office or the courthouse. In this Tax Deed Tuesday video, I share my screen and show you how I use RealAuction, a vendor that runs online auctions for counties, to see which counties sell online and what's coming up for auction.

When I recorded this, RealAuction's client list showed the counties that used its sites, by state, and the type of auction each county hosted: tax deeds, foreclosures, or both. If the county you want isn't on the list, that doesn't mean it has no auction. It means the county holds the sale in person or uses a different system, so go to that county and find out where it posts its tax deed sales.

From there, I open a county's tax deed site, point you to the start here page and the frequently asked questions, and walk through the bidder registration form. When I recorded this in May 2020, a lot of counties had pushed their auctions back because of COVID. The first county I opened had nothing on its calendar, so I used the jump to button to switch to Brevard County, Florida, which had an auction coming up.

On the calendar, the difference between the number of properties first listed and the number still scheduled tells you how many were removed or redeemed. Then I click the parcel ID on a few properties to check the property appraiser's record. One listing said vacant residential land, but the photo looked like there was a house on it, and the photo was 13 years old. That's why you check the property's use and description before you bid.

If the property type you want isn't on this month's list, don't get discouraged. Come back next month. This strategy takes research, patience and consistency.

*Tax liens* are often pitched as a *passive way to earn double-digit returns* from investments that are *backed by real estate.*

 

This is only _half_ true.

 

While these investments *average 13%-18% annual returns,* they may actually be one of the _least_ passive investing strategies. With roughly *20 years of experience as a real estate investor, attorney, and title professional, Stephen Morel* understands all that this strategy entails better than most.

 

The truth is that most investors are thinking about these investments the wrong way. *Tax liens aren’t a shortcut to acquiring cheap properties.* In fact, only 1% of these properties ever get foreclosed on. Rather, *tax lien investing is a yield play.* Unfortunately, due to the *complexity surrounding these investments, institutional investors with access to large amounts of capital* have long had a stranglehold on this industry.

 

Stephen is on a mission to change that. Tony reveals how he acquires properties for as little as $4,000–$20,000—free and clear, with no mortgage or liens—using Over-the-Counter (OTC) Tax Deed Acquisitions, a strategy that bypasses competitive tax auctions. He explains how counties hold thousands of tax-defaulted properties, why most investors overlook these opportunities, and how his 14-point research system ensures he only buys profitable properties. Tony debunks common myths about tax liens, warns against bad information in the industry, and shares real-life case studies of deals where he and his students have turned small investments into huge profits. If you’re struggling to find off-market deals, this episode is a must-listen—and Tony’s FreeCrashCourse.com is the perfect place to start. 🚀


--

About Tony:

Tony Martinez is the Founder & CEO of the U.S. Tax Lien Association (USTLA), an organization that shows people how to achieve their financial goals through the power of tax lien investing.

Tony has over 33 years of expert experience investing in tax lien certificates and tax deed properties and has completed over 2,500 successful tax deed property transactions for his own portfolio and has the irrefutable public record documentation to prove it.

USTLA is the “go to” resource for top real estate investment experts as well as novices for the most credible, accurate, and up to date information on investing in tax lien certificates and tax deed properties.

Tony and his team of experts pride themselves on helping average Americans starting with limited capital enter the lucrative world of real estate investing.

segments.text: the automatic stay is an important
benefit of filing for bankruptcy
it's a rule which allows the debtor to
call a timeout from creditor collection
efforts as soon as the bankruptcy
process gets underway the automatic stay
kicks in in this presentation we'll look
at the automatic stay what it does and
how it operates an automatic stay under
Section 362 of the United States
Bankruptcy Code is a bankruptcy court
order that goes into effect as soon as
the party files for relief under any
chapter of bankruptcy it protects the
debtor and his assets from creditors to
facilitate an equitable treatment of the
creditors in the collective bankruptcy
process the state prevents creditors
from going after the party that's filed
for bankruptcy even if that creditor
received no notice of the filing when
Congress enacted section 362 of the
Bankruptcy Code in 1978 its legislative
intent behind the automatic stay was
presented as follows the automatic stay
gives the debtor a breathing spell from
his creditors it stops all collection
efforts all harassment and all
foreclosure actions it permits the
debtor to attempt a repayment or a
reorganization plan or simply to be
relieved of the financial pressures that
drove him into bankruptcy the bankruptcy
court must have an opportunity to sort
matters out and begin an orderly
administration of the estate creditors
cannot harass contact sue or generally
pester the debtor if the creditor does
so in violation of the stay its actions
are void and may be reversed by a court
the automatic stay provisions are broad
and can be applied to all types of
creditors including governmental units
this stay applies among other things to
almost all administrative proceedings
against the debtor the enforcement of
any judgment obtained before the
commencement of the case any act to
obtain possession of property of the
estate any act to create perfect or
enforce a lien against property of the
estate any act to collect assess or
recover a claim against the debtor and
the set-off
of any debt owing to the debtor let's
break down some of these circumstances
to which the automatic stay applies
first once a person files a bankruptcy
petition the automatic stay immediately
stops the bank from foreclosing on or
repossessing the debtors real or
personal property examples include the
debtors home or her car the automatic
stay doesn't allow the debtor to avoid
mortgage or car payments it temporarily
stops for
or collection proceedings but payments
and interest will continue to accrue and
the foreclosure proceedings can be
brought as soon as the automatic stay is
lifted so if one wants to keep one's
house or car in the long run
one should continue to make mortgage or
car payments even when the automatic
stay is in effect secured creditors such
as mortgage and auto financing companies
can often get relief from the automatic
stay and secure the right to proceed
which collection and foreclosure efforts
by filing a motion for relief from the
automatic stay Section 362 D of the
Bankruptcy Code discusses the grounds
for obtaining relief though these
determinations are necessarily made on a
case-by-case basis the two most common
methods for relief from the stay are
found in Section 362 d1 and 362 d2 the
first 362 d1 states that relief from the
stay may be granted for a creditor for
cause including the lack of adequate
protection of an interest in property
the adequate protection caveat exists
because bankruptcies don't happen in a
vacuum
the needs of creditors must also be
considered for example if a bank has a
lien on the debtors home the bank wants
the debtors home to preserve its value
should the home lose value due to
neglect by the debtor the bank security
interest would be harmed
examples of debtor actions that can lead
to automatic stay relief for a creditor
due to adequate protection include the
wasting of resources perhaps taking long
on necessary road trips in the case of a
car or failing to make repairs to the
roof of a house or mismanagement and
damage to the property showing that any
of these are occurring could allow a
court to lift the automatic stay and
allow foreclosure proceedings to
commence or to continue section 362 D 2
of the Bankruptcy Code also allows a
court to grant a creditor relief from
the automatic stay if the creditor can
satisfy the following two prongs one the
debtor doesn't have an equity interest
in the property that the creditor seeks
and two the property isn't necessary to
an effective reorganization if
reorganization is unlikely or the
collateral is unnecessary the collateral
will eventually be foreclosed on or sold
and its proceeds will become part of the
bankruptcy estate the automatic stay
also applies to residential lease
evictions and protects rent
who filed for bankruptcy from being
evicted from their rental property
however there are exceptions first if
the Bankruptcy Court finds that the
tenant never had the right to occupy the
leased premises in the first place then
the leased premises never become part of
the bankruptcy estate and the automatic
stay will not apply the tenant is a mere
squatter who cannot secure a right to
possess property merely by filing for
bankruptcy second a tenant can be
evicted if the landlord started the
eviction process before the bankruptcy
filing
finally the automatic stay will not
prevent an eviction if the landlord is
evicting the tenant based on
endangerment to the property or the
illegal use of controlled substances
within the property the automatic stay
will also stop utility shutoffs if the
debtor is behind on an electricity water
gas phone or other utility bill and is
under threat of having the service cut
off the automatic stay prohibits utility
companies from doing so while the stay
is in place furthermore a utility can't
refuse service or discriminate against
the debtor solely on the basis that he
has filed for bankruptcy this day isn't
they blanket protection a debtor may
have to provide adequate assurance of
payment within 20 days to prevent the
utility company from shutting off
service an adequate assurance of
payments can be a deposit letter of
credit prepayment or any evidence of a
promise that the debtor will make
regular payments to the utility
providers the automatic stay even
prevents a government agency from
recovering an overpayment of public
benefits such as unemployment or welfare
payments normally the agency is entitled
to collect the overpayment of benefits
out of a debtors future check but once
the debtor files for bankruptcy the
automatic stay can stop an agency from
recouping the overpayments the agency
may recoup overpayment in future
eligibility payments once this day is
lifted the automatic stay stops almost
all entities from instituting wage
garnishments until the stay is lifted a
wage garnishment is a court order
requiring an employer to withhold
certain amounts of an employee's pay and
distribute that amount to a creditor
named in the court order the state does
not however stop garnishments to pay
spousal support and child support orders
also after the debtor files for
bankruptcy a creditor can continue to
litigate a pending lawsuit against the
debtor to
on claims that arose before the filing
if the creditor files a lawsuit against
the debtor prior to the petition date
and the suit simply halts pending the
bankruptcy proceeding typically a debtor
who's a defendant in a pre petition
litigation will provide written notice
to the court and the other parties that
the action must be stayed shortly after
it files the bankruptcy petition in a
real-life example Mammoet starna 'the an
engineering company that specializes in
design and construction of giant
observation wheels and structures filed
for chapter 11 bankruptcy in December of
2017 prior to filing the petition New
York wheel had sued star Neth in May of
for project delays and recovery of costs
associated with the 580 million dollar
630 foot tall giant New York wheel
attraction that star natha's to build on
Staten Island in its bankruptcy filing
starting stated that an automatic stay
applies and protects it from creditors
and shields it from the New York wheel
lawsuit applying law to these facts it
appears that the automatic stay does
apply and will halt at least temporarily
New York wheels lawsuit against Arnoff
because the lawsuit was filed prior to
the bankruptcy petitions filing the
automatic stay is a powerful tool to
help debtors get a breather while a
bankruptcy proceeding goes forward in
another presentation we'll continue
discussing the automatic stay and its
limitations

would be harmed examples of debtor actions that can lead to automatic stay relief for a creditor due to adequate protection include the wasting of resources perhaps taking long on necessary road trips in the case of a car or failing to make repairs to the roof of a house or mismanagement and damage to the property showing that any of these are occurring could allow a court to lift the automatic stay and allow foreclosure proceedings to commence or to continue section 362 D 2 of the Bankruptcy Code also allows a court to grant a creditor relief from the automatic stay if the creditor can satisfy the following two prongs one the debtor doesn't have an equity interest in the property that the creditor seeks and two the property isn't necessary to an effective reorganization if reorganization is unlikely or the collateral is unnecessary the collateral will eventually be foreclosed on or sold and its proceeds will become part of the bankruptcy estate the automatic stay also applies to residential lease evictions and protects rent who filed for bankruptcy from being evicted from their rental property however there are exceptions first if the Bankruptcy Court finds that the tenant never had the right to occupy the leased premises in the first place then the leased premises never become part of the bankruptcy estate and the automatic stay will not apply the tenant is a mere squatter who cannot secure a right to possess property merely by filing for bankruptcy second a tenant can be evicted if the landlord started the eviction process before the bankruptcy filing finally the automatic stay will not prevent an eviction if the landlord is evicting the tenant based on endangerment to the property or the illegal use of controlled substances within the property the automatic stay will also stop utility shutoffs if the debtor is behind on an electricity water gas phone or other utility bill and is under threat of having the service cut off the automatic stay prohibits utility companies from doing so while the stay is in place furthermore a utility can't refuse service or discriminate against the debtor solely on the basis that he has filed for bankruptcy this day isn't they blanket protection a debtor may have to provide adequate assurance of payment within 20 days to prevent the utility company from shutting off service an adequate assurance of payments can be a deposit letter of credit prepayment or any evidence of a promise that the debtor will make regular payments to the utility providers the automatic stay even prevents a government agency from recovering an overpayment of public benefits such as unemployment or welfare payments normally the agency is entitled to collect the overpayment of benefits out of a debtors future check but once the debtor files for bankruptcy the automatic stay can stop an agency from recouping the overpayments the agency may recoup overpayment in future eligibility payments once this day is lifted the automatic stay stops almost all entities from instituting wage garnishments until the stay is lifted a wage garnishment is a court order requiring an employer to withhold certain amounts of an employee's pay and distribute that amount to a creditor named in the court order the state does not however stop garnishments to pay spousal support and child support orders also after the debtor files for bankruptcy a creditor can continue to litigate a pending lawsuit against the debtor to on claims that arose before the filing if the creditor files a lawsuit against the debtor prior to the petition date and the suit simply halts pending the bankruptcy proceeding typically a debtor who's a defendant in a pre petition litigation will provide written notice to the court and the other parties that the action must be stayed shortly after it files the bankruptcy petition in a real-life example Mammoet starna 'the an engineering company that specializes in design and construction of giant observation wheels and structures filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy in December of 2017 prior to filing the petition New York wheel had sued star Neth in May of 2017 for project delays and recovery of costs associated with the 580 million dollar 630 foot tall giant New York wheel attraction that star natha's to build on Staten Island in its bankruptcy filing starting stated that an automatic stay applies and protects it from creditors and shields it from the New York wheel lawsuit applying law to these facts it appears that the automatic stay does apply and will halt at least temporarily New York wheels lawsuit against Arnoff because the lawsuit was filed prior to the bankruptcy petitions filing the automatic stay is a powerful tool to help debtors get a breather while a bankruptcy proceeding goes forward in another presentation we'll continue discussing the automatic stay and its limitations

Today I want to answer another  question we get from a lot of people.  What are Over the Counter or OTC liens

Over the counter liens, also known as OTC liens sound, when you listen to some gurus, to be the way to go.  All you do is send a check to the county and they sell you a lien.
What are they?  These are liens that did not sell at the tax sale.  The question you have to ask is why they did not sell.

Some gurus will tell you that everybody ran out of money and this why they didn't sell.  This is not likely and you can check it quickly...if that were true all the OTC liens would be at the end of the sale. I have never found that to be the case.

Over the counter or OTC liens are liens that nobody wanted to buy at the sale
Why didn't they sell?  In most cases because they had major problems that very bright buyers did not want to deal with.

You may find decent vacant land on an otc list but it is unlikely you will find any decent improved parcels.  Be very careful.

To sum it all up.

Remember, when you buy an OTC lien you are buying something that nobody else wanted...that is a hint!

You must be very careful when buying over the counter tax liens, never buy one unless you know exactly what you are getting.

Ignore the gurus, they are not the ones who will lose the money
