metadata.title: Web GIS Tutorial: Parcels, Map Layers, Analysis and Utility Networks
metadata.author: All Things Spatial
metadata.shortDescription:
One parcel in Livonia, Michigan, six public data sources, and a utility network you can trace and edit. This tour walks through a working web GIS: how to read a parcel report, which checks are live services and which are dated snapshots, why a layer disappears at the wrong scale, what an NDVI or heat map is actually worth, how a valve trace works, and two ways to build the same app (ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript vs ArcGIS Experience Builder).
Open the app: https://studio.allthingsspatial.io/map?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=STU-S01E09
Full walkthrough and what it does not do: https://www.allthingsspatial.io/pages/studio/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=STU-S01E09

Open the Studio: https://studio.allthingsspatial.io/map?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=STU-S01E09

Try it:
- Bookmarks, then Flood Zone, then the Rouge River floodway parcel: read the six checks, then Export PDF.
- Layers: turn the aerial on at the city extent, then zoom in past 1:36,922.
- Analysis: compare the two NDVI designs (1988-2025 vs 2013-2025).
- Editing Examples: Trace a water valve, then draw a gas main down Veri Court (the sandbox resets nightly).

Chapters
0:00 Preview: one valve, one trace
0:48 Every parcel in Livonia, Michigan
1:45 Six checks: live services vs dated snapshots
2:31 Flood, soils and wetlands on one parcel
5:06 The parcel report (PDF)
5:36 Reading the map: layers and scale
6:44 Layers vs computations, features vs map images
8:06 Vegetation change with NDVI (1988-2025)
9:57 Site suitability is a policy choice
10:32 Urban heat from Landsat (July 2024)
11:13 Crash heat map: density is not a hot spot
11:52 Tracing a water network
14:46 Editing a gas network with domains
17:07 Search, bookmarks, scale and custom web tools
19:26 Coded app vs Experience Builder

Need parcel diligence, utility GIS or a web map built on your own data? Book a working session with All Things Spatial: https://www.allthingsspatial.io/pages/book.html?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=STU-S01E09

More ATS apps: https://www.allthingsspatial.io/pages/apps.html?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=STU-S01E09
Data sources: https://www.allthingsspatial.io/pages/sources.html?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=STU-S01E09
Blog: https://www.allthingsspatial.io/pages/blog.html?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=STU-S01E09
All Things Spatial: https://www.allthingsspatial.io?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=STU-S01E09

Data in the Studio (publisher, vintage; "live" = queried when you click)
- Parcels: City of Livonia parcels (Wayne County, MI), 38,178 parcels, an ATS-hosted copy of the city cadastre (not authoritative; confirm with the city or county). Public records.
- Flood: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL), layer 28 - live
- Slope: USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), ~1 m - live
- Wildfire: NIFC current wildfire incidents (Esri USA Wildfires feed) - live; USFS Wildfire Hazard Potential, version 2023 (RDS-2015-0047-4), a static class for Livonia (very low).
- Soils: USDA NRCS SSURGO (MI163) v12 (2026-08-31) - ATS-hosted Livonia snapshot, taken 2026-11-06.
- Wetlands: USFWS National Wetlands Inventory - ATS-hosted Livonia snapshot, 2026-06-15.
- Environmental: EPA Facility Registry Service + ECHO - ATS-hosted Livonia snapshot, 2026-06-15.
- Aerial: Wayne County GIS 6-inch aerial imagery, flown 2020 (live tile service); fallback: City of Livonia / SEMCOG 6-inch, flown 2015
- Traffic crashes: SEMCOG crash locations (crash2025_10year), Livonia, 2016-2025 - live, with a bundled fallback dated 2026-11-06
- Vegetation change: USGS Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 surface reflectance via Microsoft Planetary Computer; scenes 1988-09-10 (Landsat 5), 2013-07-13 (Landsat 8), 2025-07-14 (Landsat 8), 2025-07-22 (Landsat 9).
- Urban heat: USGS Landsat 8 Collection 2 Level-2 Surface Temperature (ST_B10), scene 2024-07-27.
- Zoning, voting precincts, refuse pickup: City of Livonia GIS layers.
- Utility networks (water, sewer, gas, electric) and 311 reports: synthetic ATS demo data over a real subdivision; a public sandbox that resets nightly. No real utility's asset data.

Sources (Esri), as of Nov 2026
- ArcGIS Online, Custom web tools (user types, roles, Run web tools privilege, 70 credits per hour by the minute, no public sharing)
- ArcGIS Pro, Subnetwork controllers / utility network vocabulary
- ArcGIS Pro, Isolation trace
- ArcGIS Experience Builder, Experience deployment (download and host a Developer Edition app)
Other sources
- 49 CFR 192.3 (MAOP) and 192.455 (external corrosion control), eCFR

#GIS #ArcGIS #Geospatial #AllThingsSpatial #WebGIS

segments.text: In Trace mode, click one gate valve, and the panel counts the service connections
that lose water.
In this demo network, 28 service connections go dry when that one valve closes.
The same app checks one Livonia parcel against six public data sources, each with
its source and its date.
This tour starts with that parcel.
It moves through the city's layers and four analysis tools, and ends on a network
you can trace and edit.
This is every parcel in the City of Livonia, Michigan: 38,178 of them in the ATS
copy, as of November 2026.
They are a hosted copy of the city cadastre, and the City of Livonia holds the
official record.
This is ATS GIS Studio, a working web GIS built on public data.
Every check and every layer names its source, its date, and how far to trust it.
Open the bookmarks, choose the flood zone group, and pick a parcel in the Rouge
River floodway.
The card shows where this parcel sits within Livonia, on the river corridor.
The panel starts with the parcel record: who owns it, where the tax bill goes, and
how much land there is.
This dataset has no assessed value and no deed history, and the panel states that.
Below the record are six independent checks, and each one names its source and the
time it was checked.
Three of them ask an agency's own service at the moment you click.
Flood is FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer.
Slope comes from USGS 3DEP elevation.
Wildfire reads NIFC's current incidents and the Forest Service's 2023 Wildfire
Hazard Potential class for Livonia.
The other three read copies that ATS hosts, and each copy is dated.
Wetlands and the EPA records are snapshots dated June 15, 2026.
Soils is a snapshot of the August 2026 soil survey, taken November 6, 2026.
Flood comes first: this parcel is in Zone AE, with a mapped floodway.
A base flood elevation is mapped here, and the floodway is the channel and nearby
land that must stay clear of obstructions.
An official flood zone determination is a separate document.
Soils come from the SSURGO survey of the USDA's Natural Resources Conservation
Service.
The survey classifies each soil for specific uses, and the use that matters here is
dwellings with basements.
For this parcel, the soil check comes back very limited.
The survey is mapped at scales of about 1:12,000 to 1:24,000.
It describes a soil map unit, not the spot where a foundation would go.
Wetlands come from the US Fish and Wildlife Service's National Wetlands Inventory.
In the June 2026 snapshot, the largest wetland polygon touching this parcel is just
over 28 acres.
Most of it lies along the river, off the parcel.
Adding every polygon that touches the lot would report more wetland than the parcel
has land.
So the check clips every wetland to the parcel, dissolves the overlaps, and measures
what is left.
The inventory itself is non-regulatory, and a jurisdictional call comes from the
Army Corps of Engineers.
Environmental reads EPA's Facility Registry Service and its enforcement records,
counting regulated facilities within about half a mile.
A regulated facility holds a permit or reports to EPA.
Regulated does not mean contaminated.
The count helps decide whether to order a Phase I environmental site assessment.
Slope is measured at about one meter.
At that detail, one curb or ditch bank reads in the tens of degrees.
So the check uses the 95th percentile, the slope that 95% of the parcel is gentler
than.
The 2023 wildfire hazard class is very low across the whole city.
A built-out suburb has almost no wildland fuel.
The nearest active fire comes from NIFC's live list, which changes daily.
The floodway and largest wetland follow the river; very limited soils cover much of
the city.
All six roll up into one overall call, RED, AMBER or GREEN, as a triage flag.
How much each check counts is a policy choice, not a fact in the data.
When the six sections finish, Export PDF writes a Parcel Diligence Report.
It carries the record and the six checks with their sources and times.
It also lists which sources were live and which were dated snapshots.
It ends with the same caution the panel gives: not a substitute for professional due
diligence.
It flags which parcels need a closer look.
That closer look is still a survey, an environmental assessment and a site visit.
The Layers tab shows the same data as patterns across the whole city.
Turn Soils on.
It is the same survey that called that one parcel very limited, now drawn across the
city.
The wet ground follows the watercourses, and the parcels that came back red sit on
the same piece of geography.
Add wetlands and environmental alongside it.
The wetlands follow the same watercourses as the wet soils.
Each layer card lists the scale where that layer starts to draw.
Outside that scale range, the layer does not draw.
Turn on the aerial imagery.
The switch says on, and nothing appears.
The card shows this layer draws at 1:36,922 and closer, and the map is zoomed out
past that.
Zoom in past that scale, and the aerial draws.
At city scale, six-inch imagery holds far more detail than the screen can show, so
the service waits until you zoom in.
Each card also has a "Zoom to layer" button.
The Parcel tab runs six checks, and the Layers tab lists all six.
Three are hosted snapshots, and flood, slope and wildfire draw live from public
online services.
The check scores are not layers: each one is computed when you click.
A computation happens on demand, for the one polygon you asked about.
The parcels arrive as features: individual polygons your browser holds, which is why
clicking one returns its record.
The flood layer arrives as a map image: a picture drawn on FEMA's server and sent
back as pixels.
The browser holds no attribute table for those pixels.
Then the local layers: zoning, voting precincts and refuse pickup, the city's own
operational records.
The aerial is six-inch imagery from Wayne County, flown in 2020.
The tile service is live, but the picture is one 2020 flight.
It stays the same until the county flies again.
The flood layer on the same map is FEMA's effective map, and it changes whenever
FEMA revises it.
Last on the list are the ownership insights: out-of-area owners and entity-owned
parcels.
Those are not published by any agency.
They are inferred from the taxpayer's mailing city and from owner-name patterns.
The Analysis tab holds four tools: "Vegetation Change", "Site Suitability", "Urban
Heat (LST)" and "Hot-Spot Analysis".
Each tool states its data, its dates and its method.
Start with vegetation change.
This tool maps NDVI, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index.
Healthy plants reflect near-infrared light and absorb red, so NDVI is high where
growth is vigorous and low where it is not.
Difference two dates, and you have a map of where the city gained and lost
vegetation.
The imagery is Landsat, from the US Geological Survey: Collection 2 surface
reflectance, already corrected for the atmosphere.
Next, the comparison period offers two designs.
The long design runs from September 1988 to July 2025.
It reports a mean change of plus 0.058, with about 36% of the city greener.
The short design runs from July 2013 to July 2025, and reports minus 0.023.
The two results differ because they cover different spans.
By 2013 the canopy was already mature, so the recent decade reads as modest loss
from infill.
The long design also starts on Landsat 5 and ends on Landsat 8 and 9.
Different instruments, with different calibration, can inflate the size of the
change.
The short design uses the same instrument at both ends.
So on the long map, read the direction of change, green or red, but not its size.
On the short map, the size of the change can be compared as well.
Next, site suitability.
Six factors, flood, soils, wetlands, environmental, slope and wildfire, are each set
to 0, 50 or 100 on every parcel.
The weights are yours, and the map recolors in the browser as you move the sliders.
A suitability map shows your weights applied to the data, and different weights give
a different map.
Wildfire is very low across the city, so weighting it does not change the map.
"Reset to Balanced" puts the weights back.
Urban heat is land-surface temperature from Landsat 8's thermal band, on a clear
afternoon: July 27, 2024.
Land-surface temperature is the heat of the ground surface, not the air temperature.
It is what the roofs, the pavement and the ground were radiating back that
afternoon.
On the July 2024 scene, the hottest readings reach about 137 degrees Fahrenheit, on
the parking lots.
The coolest readings, around 80, are tree canopy, parks and the river corridor.
Beside the vegetation map, the hottest areas match the areas with the least canopy.
The last tool is a heat map of Livonia traffic crashes from 2016 to 2025, from
SEMCOG.
It is weighted, so fatal and serious-injury crashes count for more than
property-damage crashes.
The warm cores are the corridors and intersections carrying the injuries.
This is a kernel density surface, and it shows where points pile up.
It is not a statistical hot-spot test, so there is no significance in it and no
confidence level.
A true hot-spot statistic, Getis-Ord Gi*, is a different calculation, and the panel
lists it as planned, not as present.
The Editing Examples tab holds sample utility networks you can inspect, trace and
edit.
Five slots sit on one switcher: water, sewer, gas, electric and 311 Reports.
The four networks can be inspected, traced and edited, and 311 Reports is a point
layer you add to.
The networks are synthetic, a fictional system modelled over a real subdivision, and
not any real utility's asset data.
Water has four layers: mains, service lines, valves and shutoffs, and hydrants.
Sewer has five layers, because sewer runs on gravity, and gravity brings its own
asset classes.
Choose Inspect and click a water valve.
The inspector lists diameter, install year, status and turns to close.
Turns to close is how many turns of the operating nut seat the valve, so a crew can
confirm it closed.
The expected count depends on the valve's size.
A field count that disagrees with the record points to a seized valve or a broken
stem.
Now choose Trace, and click a gate valve on a main.
The map recolors, and the panel counts the service connections that lose water.
The count is service connections, not customers.
One connection can feed a duplex or an apartment building, and utilities keep those
two numbers apart.
In a looped grid, closing one valve rarely isolates a section.
Crews close the set of valves that bounds the segment, often three to five at a
cross or a tee.
If one will not seat, they work outward.
An isolation trace finds that valve set, and the connections that lose water when it
closes.
"Reset (reopen all)" opens every valve again.
Now compare the two point symbols.
The blue circle is a gate valve on a main, an isolation valve that works as part of
a set.
The blue square is a curb stop: the utility's shutoff for a single service, in a
buried box at the property line.
On the map, only the symbol tells them apart.
So each symbol is set by asset type, and crews rely on it to find the right shutoff.
On electric, open a switch on a primary line, and the service connections cut off
from the substation turn red and are counted.
The panel states its method: a spatial-graph trace, inferred from coincident
geometry, with the substation as the circuit feed.
In an ArcGIS Utility Network, the feed is a subnetwork controller, such as a
reservoir, a substation or a circuit breaker.
A utility network stores connectivity in the data model, instead of deriving it from
geometry every time you trace.
Two pipes that look connected but are not will give a wrong trace result.
The panel states that this is a public sandbox, and the data resets nightly to its
original state.
Veri Court, the cul-de-sac, has no utilities yet, and the editing steps add them
there.
Switch to gas, choose Inspect, and click a distribution main.
The pressure system reads Intermediate: operating pressure 10 psig, maximum
allowable operating pressure 60.
Maximum allowable operating pressure is the most the pipe may be operated at, and
operating pressure is what it carries today.
Every gas main has a coating field, because buried steel corrodes.
Federal pipeline safety rules require corrosion control on buried steel, and on a
plastic main the coating reads not applicable.
Now choose Edit.
This is the ArcGIS Editor widget, bound to the gas service.
Pick the Gas Mains template and draw a main down Veri Court.
With snapping on, the first vertex lands on the existing main, so the new line
touches the network.
Pressure system is a pick-list, not a text box, because the field carries a coded
value domain.

videos.full_text: In Trace mode, click one gate valve, and the panel counts the service connections that lose water. In this demo network, 28 service connections go dry when that one valve closes. The same app checks one Livonia parcel against six public data sources, each with its source and its date. This tour starts with that parcel. It moves through the city's layers and four analysis tools, and ends on a network you can trace and edit. This is every parcel in the City of Livonia, Michigan: 38,178 of them in the ATS copy, as of November 2026. They are a hosted copy of the city cadastre, and the City of Livonia holds the official record. This is ATS GIS Studio, a working web GIS built on public data. Every check and every layer names its source, its date, and how far to trust it. Open the bookmarks, choose the flood zone group, and pick a parcel in the Rouge River floodway. The card shows where this parcel sits within Livonia, on the river corridor. The panel starts with the parcel record: who owns it, where the tax bill goes, and how much land there is. This dataset has no assessed value and no deed history, and the panel states that. Below the record are six independent checks, and each one names its source and the time it was checked. Three of them ask an agency's own service at the moment you click. Flood is FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer. Slope comes from USGS 3DEP elevation. Wildfire reads NIFC's current incidents and the Forest Service's 2023 Wildfire Hazard Potential class for Livonia. The other three read copies that ATS hosts, and each copy is dated. Wetlands and the EPA records are snapshots dated June 15, 2026. Soils is a snapshot of the August 2026 soil survey, taken November 6, 2026. Flood comes first: this parcel is in Zone AE, with a mapped floodway. A base flood elevation is mapped here, and the floodway is the channel and nearby land that must stay clear of obstructions. An official flood zone determination is a separate document. Soils come from the SSURGO survey of the USDA's Natural Resources Conservation Service. The survey classifies each soil for specific uses, and the use that matters here is dwellings with basements. For this parcel, the soil check comes back very limited. The survey is mapped at scales of about 1:12,000 to 1:24,000. It describes a soil map unit, not the spot where a foundation would go. Wetlands come from the US Fish and Wildlife Service's National Wetlands Inventory. In the June 2026 snapshot, the largest wetland polygon touching this parcel is just over 28 acres. Most of it lies along the river, off the parcel. Adding every polygon that touches the lot would report more wetland than the parcel has land. So the check clips every wetland to the parcel, dissolves the overlaps, and measures what is left. The inventory itself is non-regulatory, and a jurisdictional call comes from the Army Corps of Engineers. Environmental reads EPA's Facility Registry Service and its enforcement records, counting regulated facilities within about half a mile. A regulated facility holds a permit or reports to EPA. Regulated does not mean contaminated. The count helps decide whether to order a Phase I environmental site assessment. Slope is measured at about one meter. At that detail, one curb or ditch bank reads in the tens of degrees. So the check uses the 95th percentile, the slope that 95% of the parcel is gentler than. The 2023 wildfire hazard class is very low across the whole city. A built-out suburb has almost no wildland fuel. The nearest active fire comes from NIFC's live list, which changes daily. The floodway and largest wetland follow the river; very limited soils cover much of the city. All six roll up into one overall call, RED, AMBER or GREEN, as a triage flag. How much each check counts is a policy choice, not a fact in the data. When the six sections finish, Export PDF writes a Parcel Diligence Report. It carries the record and the six checks with their sources and times. It also lists which sources were live and which were dated snapshots. It ends with the same caution the panel gives: not a substitute for professional due diligence. It flags which parcels need a closer look. That closer look is still a survey, an environmental assessment and a site visit. The Layers tab shows the same data as patterns across the whole city. Turn Soils on. It is the same survey that called that one parcel very limited, now drawn across the city. The wet ground follows the watercourses, and the parcels that came back red sit on the same piece of geography. Add wetlands and environmental alongside it. The wetlands follow the same watercourses as the wet soils. Each layer card lists the scale where that layer starts to draw. Outside that scale range, the layer does not draw. Turn on the aerial imagery. The switch says on, and nothing appears. The card shows this layer draws at 1:36,922 and closer, and the map is zoomed out past that. Zoom in past that scale, and the aerial draws. At city scale, six-inch imagery holds far more detail than the screen can show, so the service waits until you zoom in. Each card also has a "Zoom to layer" button. The Parcel tab runs six checks, and the Layers tab lists all six. Three are hosted snapshots, and flood, slope and wildfire draw live from public online services. The check scores are not layers: each one is computed when you click. A computation happens on demand, for the one polygon you asked about. The parcels arrive as features: individual polygons your browser holds, which is why clicking one returns its record. The flood layer arrives as a map image: a picture drawn on FEMA's server and sent back as pixels. The browser holds no attribute table for those pixels. Then the local layers: zoning, voting precincts and refuse pickup, the city's own operational records. The aerial is six-inch imagery from Wayne County, flown in 2020. The tile service is live, but the picture is one 2020 flight. It stays the same until the county flies again. The flood layer on the same map is FEMA's effective map, and it changes whenever FEMA revises it. Last on the list are the ownership insights: out-of-area owners and entity-owned parcels. Those are not published by any agency. They are inferred from the taxpayer's mailing city and from owner-name patterns. Healthy plants reflect near-infrared light and absorb red, so NDVI is high where growth is vigorous and low where it is not. The weights are yours, and the map recolors in the browser as you move the sliders. A suitability map shows your weights applied to the data, and different weights give a different map. The last tool is a heat map of Livonia traffic crashes from 2016 to 2025, from SEMCOG. It is weighted, so fatal and serious-injury crashes count for more than property-damage crashes. It is not a statistical hot-spot test, so there is no significance in it and no confidence level. Sewer has five layers, because sewer runs on gravity, and gravity brings its own asset classes. Choose Inspect and click a water valve. The inspector lists diameter, install year, status and turns to close. Turns to close is how many turns of the operating nut seat the valve, so a crew can confirm it closed. The expected count depends on the valve's size. A field count that disagrees with the record points to a seized valve or a broken stem. Now choose Trace, and click a gate valve on a main. The map recolors, and the panel counts the service connections that lose water. The count is service connections, not customers. One connection can feed a duplex or an apartment building, and utilities keep those two numbers apart. In a looped grid, closing one valve rarely isolates a section. Crews close the set of valves that bounds the segment, often three to five at a cross or a tee. If one will not seat, they work outward. An isolation trace finds that valve set, and the connections that lose water when it closes. "Reset (reopen all)" opens every valve again. Now compare the two point symbols. The blue circle is a gate valve on a main, an isolation valve that works as part of a set. The blue square is a curb stop: the utility's shutoff for a single service, in a buried box at the property line. On the map, only the symbol tells them apart. So each symbol is set by asset type, and crews rely on it to find the right shutoff. On electric, open a switch on a primary line, and the service connections cut off from the substation turn red and are counted. The panel states its method: a spatial-graph trace, inferred from coincident geometry, with the substation as the circuit feed. In an ArcGIS Utility Network, the feed is a subnetwork controller, such as a reservoir, a substation or a circuit breaker. A utility network stores connectivity in the data model, instead of deriving it from geometry every time you trace. Two pipes that look connected but are not will give a wrong trace result. The panel states that this is a public sandbox, and the data resets nightly to its original state. Veri Court, the cul-de-sac, has no utilities yet, and the editing steps add them there. Switch to gas, choose Inspect, and click a distribution main. The pressure system reads Intermediate: operating pressure 10 psig, maximum allowable operating pressure 60. Maximum allowable operating pressure is the most the pipe may be operated at, and operating pressure is what it carries today. Every gas main has a coating field, because buried steel corrodes. Federal pipeline safety rules require corrosion control on buried steel, and on a plastic main the coating reads not applicable. Now choose Edit. This is the ArcGIS Editor widget, bound to the gas service. Pick the Gas Mains template and draw a main down Veri Court. With snapping on, the first vertex lands on the existing main, so the new line touches the network. Pressure system is a pick-list, not a text box, because the field carries a coded value domain. metadata.title: Esri Land Administration Latin American Webinar Series, Webinar #2 Parcel Management With GIS
metadata.author: Esri Industries
metadata.shortDescription:
Parcel mapping and management have always been critical functions in cadastral systems worldwide.  Each organization is different.  Some are starting with new parcel mapping beginning with only imagery.  Others are collecting new parcels in the field with GNSS.  And others are using digital data in various conditions of accuracy and completeness.  The parcel fabric is a purpose-built capability that manages parcel data integrity, survey record, history, 3D, and more.  The parcel fabric is configurable to work with many unique requirements.  This webinar will show how the parcel fabric delivers mapping efficiencies and helps improve data quality whether you’re just getting started or if you are managing an enterprise cadastral system.

IRS Tax Lien Explained - Credit, Property, and Release Options

metadata.title: Quick Tips | Filling Out IRS Form 12277: Application for Withdrawal of Federal Tax Lien
metadata.author: Canopy
metadata.shortDescription: Need help filling out IRS form 12277? The 12277 can be complicated, but we've got the information you need to get your lien withdrawn the first time.

segments.text: Hi, and welcome to another IRS forms video.
Today we’re tackling IRS Form 12277, Application for Withdrawal of Federal Tax Lien.
Getting the IRS to withdraw a lien can be a huge benefit for your clients.
Let’s take a look at what that takes, and how you can use Form 12277 to make it happen.
Tip 1: How to Resolve IRS Liens and When to Use Form 12277
When a taxpayer lets their tax debt go unaddressed for too long, the IRS will respond by placing
a lien on their assets.
By issuing a lien, the IRS is asserting a legal claim to a taxpayer’s property
as a security against the tax debt.
That claim, if left unchecked, will end with the IRS seizing the taxpayer’s assets—
bank accounts, valuables, real assets with equity—in an attempt to fulfill the outstanding tax debt.
The IRS liens can be resolved in two different ways—release and withdrawal.
A lien release gets rid of most of the immediate effects of a lien.
Because the IRS no longer has any interest in the assets,
your client may sell or transfer their assets at will.
The IRS will release a lien 30 days after the tax debt has either been satisfied through
an installment agreement or Offer in Compromise.
A lien will also automatically be released 30 days after the collections statute expiration date,
or if the tax debt is discharged in bankruptcy.
A lien release, however, does not erase all of the effects of a lien.
The lien will remain on the taxpayer’s credit history unless the IRS withdraws the lien.
A withdrawal allows the lien to be removed from the client’s credit history as if it had never been issued.
IRS Form 12277 is the form you will use to request that withdrawal.
Tip 2: Reasons for Lien Withdrawal Getting a lien withdrawn is obviously the
preferable option, so how do you know if your client qualifies to have their lien withdrawn?
Line 11, of Form 12277, lists four reasons the IRS will consider withdrawing the lien.
Reason #1- “The Notice of Federal Tax Lien was filed
prematurely or not in accordance with IRS procedures.”
The IRS will withdraw the lien if the tax that eventually prompted the lien was assessed
in error, or if the lien was filed without giving the taxpayer proper notice.
This is extremely rare, as the IRS has multiple fail-safes in place to avoid these kinds of mistakes.
However, mistakes do still happen, and the IRS will withdraw the lien if you can prove it.
#2- “The taxpayer entered into an installment agreement to satisfy the liability for which
the lien was imposed and the agreement did not provide for
a Notice of Federal Tax Lien to be filed.”
This is the most common method of getting a lien withdrawn.
The IRS Fresh Start Program allows the IRS to withdraw a lien if the taxpayer has entered
into a Direct Debit Installment Agreement.
In order to qualify for withdrawal, the taxpayer must have filed all required tax returns
for the last three years and must be current with any estimated tax payments.
#3- “Withdrawal will facilitate the collection of the tax.”
Because a tax lien is so detrimental to a taxpayer’s credit, it will often affect
their ability to borrow money.
If the IRS can be convinced that withdrawing a lien will allow the taxpayer to borrow money
and pay off their tax debt, they will likely withdraw the lien.
#4- “The taxpayer, or the Taxpayer Advocate acting on behalf of the taxpayer, believes
withdrawal is in the best interest of the taxpayer and the government.”
This option is hard to quantify exactly because “best interest” is hard to nail down.
But according to a former IRS Revenue Officer who now works at Canopy, the advice commonly
given at the IRS was, “Don’t do anything that would land you
on the front page of the local paper.”
Basically, the IRS doesn’t want to get caught putting a lien on the house of the 90-year-old
widow living on Social Security.
If you’ve got a situation you think merits special consideration, check this box on Form 12277.
Tip Three: Attach Form 668(Y), Notice of Federal Tax Lien
Line nine of Form 12277 instructs you to “Attach copy of the Form 668(Y), Notice of Federal Tax Lien, if available,”
or provide information about the notice.
Attaching a copy of the actual notice will be a huge time saver for you, the IRS, and your client.
Even if your client doesn’t have a copy of the lien, you can often get a copy from
your local IRS office without too much hassle.
Well, that’s all we have for you today.
Be sure to check out our other videos for all your IRS form filling needs.
Also, please like the video and subscribe to be notified when we put more helpful videos out.
If you have any questions or suggestions for other forms we should cover, let us know in the comments.
You know what's easier than watching form videos on Youtube?
Letting Canopy fill out the forms for you.

metadata.title: Investing in Tax Liens with a Self Directed IRA
metadata.author: CamaPlan Self Directed IRA
metadata.shortDescription:
By popular demand, Carl Fischer teaches on investing in tax liens using a self-directed IRA. He will be covering a list of topics including:
• Comparing Tax Lien Vs Certificate and Tax Deed
• Discussing the process of purchasing tax liens
• Identify entities for purchase of tax deeds and tax liens/certificates
• Evaluate pros and cons of using different entities
• Examine a step by step approach to utilize your IRA/401k
• Review custodian fees

Carl Fischer is a Cornell University graduate and third generation real estate developer. Carl began his investing career in the 1970’s when he was employed as a rocket scientist at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida. He is presently one of the founders and principals of CamaPlan self-directed IRA.

metadata.author: NuView Trust
metadata.shortDescription:
Investing in tax liens and tax deeds with a self-directed IRA can help diversify your portfolio and get real estate exposure without investing in a property. So what are tax liens and tax deeds and how can a person benefit from them?
 
Property taxes continue to grow in thousands of counties across the country. In order to fund the necessary county services, many states collect delinquent property taxes through tax lien and tax deed auctions. Each state holds these auctions a bit differently, but in all cases, these tax deeds or tax liens can be purchased within a self-directed IRA.
 
Buying tax lien certificates can be a breath of fresh air for most investors. The tax lien strategy is simple. The returns are great, and they’re guaranteed with real assets! However, investors have to know what they are doing and take the time to research the properties upon which they buy liens.

Learn more about NuView Trust and the power of self-directed investing by downloading our free self-directed IRA E-Guide: https://bit.ly/2LPwjTL

metadata.title: Tax Lien Investing for Beginners: 8-18% Interest? Risks & Auction Mistakes
metadata.author: Smart Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
Tax lien investing sounds almost too good to be true: buy a county tax lien certificate and earn interest while the property owner pays you back. But can you really earn 8% to 18% interest — and what are the risks nobody talks about? This beginner guide gives you the honest answer.

We explain how tax lien investing actually works: when a property owner falls behind on property taxes, the county sells the lien at a public auction, the investor pays the back taxes, and the owner has a redemption period to repay with interest. Statutory rates vary by state and can reach 8% to 36%, but in competitive auctions realistic returns for individual investors are often 6% to 12%. Around 95% of liens are redeemed, so most investors earn interest rather than acquiring the property — and your money can be locked up for 1 to 3 years.

You will also learn the beginner mistakes that cost real money: skipping due diligence on the property, ignoring senior liens and code violations, overbidding in competitive auctions, and misunderstanding redemption periods and foreclosure rules, which vary by state and county. We cover how to find county auctions, how to research a lien before bidding, and how much to start with. Tax lien investing can be a useful fixed-income strategy — but only with careful research and realistic expectations.

metadata.title: Tax Enforcement After Tyler v. Hennepin County
metadata.author: The Devine Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode Summary:
In this episode of Devine Intervention: Shedding Light on Illinois Property Tax, host Nora Devine, a seasoned property tax attorney, is joined by Lynnette Lockwitz, managing partner at Reiter Law. They delve into the implications of a pivotal U.S. Supreme Court case, Tyler v. Hennepin County, which has disrupted real estate tax enforcement in Illinois. 

The discussion highlights how this ruling, which deemed the retention of excess equity held by counties, post property tax deed sale, as a Fifth Amendment “Taking,” and unconstitutional, affects the current tax enforcement mechanisms throughout similarly situated states, like Illinoist. Lynnette explains the historical context, the legal intricacies of tax sales, and the potential legislative responses being considered in Illinois. This episode is crucial for property owners, investors, and legal professionals navigating the evolving landscape of property tax deed sales in Illinois. Listeners will gain valuable insights into the potential changes and how to prepare for them.

Key Timestamps:
00:01 – Introduction
00:11 – Meet the Hosts: Nora and Lynnette
00:31 – Impact of Supreme Court Case on Illinois
01:59 – Tax Enforcement Process in Illinois
03:47 – Equity and Property Under Current System
05:03 – Overview of Tyler v. Hennepin Case
06:23 – Illinois System Ruled Unconstitutional
07:32 – Legislative Responses and Stalled Cases
08:45 – Proposals to Change Tax Enforcement
09:36 – Trends in Other States' Reforms
11:03 – Michigan Case and Surplus Calculation
14:12 – Future of Private Tax Buying in Illinois
15:56 – Advice for Transactional and Title Attorneys
17:22 – Future of Tax Sale Investments

About the Show:
Devine Intervention: Shedding Light on Illinois Property Tax is a podcast dedicated to unraveling the complexities of property tax law in Illinois. Hosted by experienced property tax attorney Nora Devine, the show offers in-depth discussions with legal experts, providing valuable insights into tax enforcement, legislative changes, and property owner rights. Whether you're a homeowner, investor, or legal professional, this podcast equips you with the knowledge to navigate the intricacies of Illinois property tax law with confidence.

For more information, visit our website:
www.thedevinelawgroup.com

#IllinoisPropertyTax #TylervHennepin #RealEstateLaw #PropertyTaxReform #TaxDeeds

videos.full_text: Welcome to Divine [music] Intervention, shedding light on Illinois property tax. Hello and welcome to Divine Intervention, shedding light on Illinois property tax. I'm Nora Divine. I've been a property tax attorney in private practice since 2005 and I've developed a statewide practice across all jurisdictions in Illinois representing all property classes. Uh today I'm joined by Lynette Lowitz. Uh, Lynette is the managing partner at Writer Law Offices and her practice is limited to tax sale and tax deed matters. Today we are discussing how a US Supreme Court case has brought real estate tax enforcement to a halt in Illinois and what the legislature and taxing officials plan to do about it. Lynette, thank you so much for joining me to talk about this timely issue. >> Thanks, Nora, for having me. Um, looking forward to talking about this topic a little bit more today. >> Great. So, can you start off by just telling us something about yourself personally and how you got into this practice area? >> So, I actually got into this practice area right out of law school um through a law school extership and I always was drawn to tax in law school. Now, however, what I'm in real estate tax is a little bit different. Um but I kind of had an affinity for it. It's very um mechanical and the topics are very unique. And while I didn't think property was a strong suit of mine um in law school, it seems like I have now um niched myself into the property world, more specifically property tax. I've been doing this for close to about 19 years now. Um, I've been in a small scale, a small uh firm with just me and my partner, Greg Ryder. So, you know, we we handle kind of all aspects of this type of property tax enforcement world. Um, whether that's with homeowners or companies, uh, banks, title companies, as well as institutional investors, which we'll talk about a little bit today. >> Great. And uh to start off, how do you describe the tax enforcement process as we've known it until now in Illinois? >> Well, the the tax enforcement mechanism right now um as we know it, it still stands firm. Um we'll get into a little bit later some of the issues that are popping up regarding it. But essentially in Illinois, if a an owner fails to pay any portion of a property tax that's due, the county treasurer can then auction off that delinquency amount at an annual auction. Uh, anyone that bids at these auctions, whether that's individual property owners, other owners, um, institutional investors, or, you know, a mom and pop company that buys a couple of these leans every year. in order to acquire those leans, they're bidding a percentage rate of what they want to get paid back on that lean. So, if I um am a $100 delinquent on my taxes and the county treasurer auctions off that $100, anyone bidding on it is going to bid a percentage rate of what they want to get paid back. The ceiling percentage rate right now in Illinois is 9% and then it goes down to 0%. If you have a successful bidder, the county then issues a certificate of purchase and then that becomes a lean. That $100 delinquency becomes a lean on the property. Then after that point in time, the owner has anywhere from 12 months to 30 months, depending on the property type, to pay that lean back. And then everyone goes back about their business if it's timely redeemed, timely timely paid back. If it's not timely redeemed, then that successful tax bidder who holds that certificate can then petition through the court system to get an actual tax deed to that property. As this uh scheme in Illinois stands today, once a tax deed is issued, um as long as certain notices are done and the courts approve it, that tax buyer then becomes the owner of the property and then can file a motion for possession and take possession of that property. >> Okay. So to the extent that there's any equity in the property once that conclusion occurs, what happens to the equity in the property under the current system? So going back to my example, if I'm $100 delinquent and that $100 gets sold, but my house is worth $100,000. Like you said, there's this equity. I only owe $100. So that leaves an a rough equity balance of $99,900. So that's equity now that that successful tax buyer who now has a deed to my property has gained that I as the homeowner have lost. So that's the current way Illinois works. um is that I'm just out that equity. There is no mechanism currently. >> And we weren't the only one, right? Weren't we? Weren't there many, many states that were operating this way? >> There were about 13 states after Tyler v. Henipin that operated this way that basically take the equity and it's not returned to the homeowner. >> Okay. And so tell us about Tyler v. Henipin. This is a US Supreme Court case out of Minnesota. >> Yes. It's a 2023 Supreme Court case. Um, it was about an older woman, Miss Tyler, who owned a condominium property, and she owed about $15,000 in delinquent taxes as well as penalty and interest. The the law in Minnesota is the government forecloses on all these tax leans. They don't auction them off to private buyers. So, the Henipin County foreclosed on that $15,000 tax lean. They ended up selling the property for $40,000 and then that excess equity surplus of $25,000 Henipin County kept. So she took this case up to the Supreme Court and the Supreme Court held that county's retention of that $25,000 is a taking under the fifth amendment takings clause because they didn't give her just compensation. So that's kind of these 13 states we're talking about all had tax enforcement mechanisms similar to Illinois and similar to Minnesota where this extra equity after a tax deed issued does not get returned to the homeowner. >> Okay. And now we have a follow-up case out of the seventh circuit court of appeals that has ruled that Illinois's uh system is likewise unconstitutional. Correct. >> Um so in that case it's it's not that the scheme as a whole is unconstitutional. So, it's it's it's just if a tax deed issues and a tax buyer takes possession of that property and doesn't return the equity surplus that you run into a constitutional issue. So, as far as the current mechanism, as I said earlier, you know, they sell the lean. As long as I pay my $100 back, there's no issue. the system's working as it's designed to work to to spur these foreclosures to spur people to pay their taxes. It's only kind of when we get to this end point of a tax deed issuing and me as the tax buyer not returning that excess equity that you now have a constitutional taking. >> Where does it stand now? I mean, the legislature has obviously been told that something needs to happen with the property tax code, otherwise it's still going to remain unconstitutional. And now you have judges that are afraid to issue orders. You have cases that are not moving forward. You have a 2003 tax sale that was supposed to happen but didn't. I mean, everything is just kind of stalled. What what is going to happen next? >> Everything is very much stalled. So, let's keep in mind Tyler v. Henipin, that ruling was in 2023, May of 2023. So, we're now coming up in Illinois on the third anniversary of that ruling coming out. And Illinois, again, is the only state that hasn't done anything. Um there's been legislation introduced. There was legislation introduced down in Springfield last session. There is a lot of legislation introduced um in this session as well. There's a couple kind of front runners that look like they might have support and might be able to go somewhere. um they are uh all a little bit different in how they kind of handle the issue, but they do all handle the issue in the sense that they do call for a return of the surplus equity to the owners. >> Okay. And some of these proposals would bring the enforcement mechanism inhouse for government and would eliminate the role of private investors. Is that right? >> Potentially. There is one bill um it is a bill that's introduced or it has the support of the Cook County Treasurer and the Cook County Board President. Um it's Senate Bill 3940 that does call for a sun sunset provision just in Cook County of private taxpayers. So essentially there's kind of a three-year currently the way the way the bill's written it's three years. So, it's kind of a three-year sunset period where private tax buyers can still um invest in these leans as well as the county. And then after that 3 years, all Cook County leans shall go to the county. And then it's going to be the county that has to kind of work through this foreclosure process of all these leans and then ultimately there would probably be some sort of judicial auction at the end. >> Okay? and of the systems out there, the 13 other systems that have changed their laws to comply with Tyler v. Henipin, um what has been the trend with the changes that they've made, if you know, >> they pretty much all have a judicial auction at the end. Um and they all still have private investors. So, okay, a lot of the states that complied after Tyler were what we call over bid states. So without getting too far into the weeds, basically you bid up to um what you think the propertyy's worth. So and then any overage that's bid on is what gets turned to the homeowner in those kind of overbid states. Whereas Illinois's, you know, you bid a percentage rate on the delinquency and that's what you're getting paid back from the homeowner. And then it's, you know, it's kind of an unrealized gain at the end when a tax buyer gets a tax deed to a property because they haven't sold it yet. Yeah, they could do some renovations. They could sell it for substantially more than what the property might have been worth when they got their tax deed. So, these are kind of the issues that are still out there even post Tyler v. Henipin County for all the jurisdictions that have even made changes to their uh schemes and mechanisms, >> right? Because the next question is how do you calculate the equity? What market value are you using? Are you using the value for which the property sold at auction, judicial sale, or are you using the value that the person flipped it for? Um, assuming no improvements were made. So, you said that last time we spoke about this, you told me that there was a case pending in Michigan that was at the US Supreme Court case and was just recently argued. And I think that's the question in that case. Um, did you listen to the arguments? What do you think of it? >> Yes, I did listen. It's a case called Pong versus Isabella County. And as you mentioned, it's it's a case that originated out of Michigan. Um, basically what Tyler failed to tell us was how the surplus is calculated, how it needs to be paid, is there any burden on the owner to actually go out and then try to, you know, have to institute anything to get the money back. Do they have to file a lawsuit? Can they just file a notice? So, these were kind of a lot of the questions that were left unanswered by Tyler. So now we have this Pong versus Isabella County case that was just heard for oral argument in the Supreme Court at the end of February and it addresses some of these issues in regards to what value is placed on a property when you're trying to realize what the surplus is. And just the brief facts of that case was there was a tax delinquency of $2,000 and change. Um, Isabella County foreclosed on it and sold the property for I I I don't have my numbers in front of me, but roughly for, let's say, $70,000. Then that second buyer who bought it at the auction 2 years later sold it for $150,000. Again, my numbers are off, but the the the pongs in that case were saying, "Well, we should get that 150 value, not the $70,000 the county got initially at that distressed auction sale. We should get something more akin to fair market value." Isabella County is saying it should be that a distressed auction sale price is adequate in determining surplus. So, while it was a little unclear how to tell what way the justices were going, they did focus a lot on whether the actual foreclosure auction process is fair. And that's a lot of the cases that come out of mortgage foreclosure. That's what they focus on, not did you get what you would get on the open market because we're not dealing with a property on the open market. We don't know the condition. Um, we don't know the improvements that have been made. >> We can't do an inspection. We can't right send an appraiser in. Yeah. So, it'll be interesting to see how that case resolves itself because a lot of the legislation in Illinois that's pending does make a mention of value being based off of fair market value. So, it it could raise a question. You know, one of the things you mentioned what's going to happen now in Illinois with private tax buying, is it going to be as lucrative as it was? I I don't know if it'll be as lucrative as some of the investors feel it is today, but a lot of investors in Illinois, it's it's kind of an interest game. You know, you're bidding on an initial interest rate on the initial delinquency amount and then if you pay subsequent taxes, you're getting additional interest on those. So, you know, the cost of money is high right now. So, where this kind of all shakes out, maybe margins shrink a little bit, but I do still think that there is value in in private investing and that the governments do have a use for it moving forward, even if currently there's legislation proposed to kind of phase that out in certain counties in Illinois. >> Gotcha. Yeah, I think it's been about the interest for a while. And um you know, I think that it's hard to get a tax deed in Cook County. It seems like the the judge has really bent over backwards to avoid giving a tax deed uh to a tax buyer. So I feel like it has been about interest for quite some time. Um so I think it'll be interesting to see how this all plays out. You'll have to come back and talk about how it's going once we have a new system in place. Um but right now what are you advising the colleagues that you have that do transactional work and title insurance attorneys? like what's the best advice that you can give them right now? >> The best advice right now is cuz as you mentioned in Cook County at least, the judges are not moving any of these cases. Um there was also a recent change to one of the application forms that has to be um given to the courts and filed with the courts and there was an addition of an equity question. Is there equity in this property? And what are kind of your proofs and support for whether there is or there isn't? with transactional attorneys and and title work. If you come across a property that has delinquent or sold taxes, an additional investigation needs to be made as far as where those tax sales stand. Um, there used to be an old adage that one year after that final redemption date, a certificate's dead, don't have to worry about it. Taxes are paid. That doesn't really hold true anymore because everything's stalled. A lot of these cases and a lot of these certificates are being told. So that one-year kind of die date from the redemption date doesn't really hold true anymore. You really have to look carefully at the underlying court case file and at the county records to make sure you know what position stands in that lean because what in in the old days used to be maybe a dead lean could still be a lean that's alive years later after the redemption date. Uh we saw this a lot during COVID and now we're kind of seeing it again um with these cases because the courts aren't acting. So definitely look out for that and with tolling. And if you do have a case where you know you're kind of running up against one of these redemption dates, definitely take maybe an extra step after the closing to make sure those taxes are paid. Um, we've had a couple cases recently where just, you know, balls are dropped somewhere and the check doesn't get there. The check gets there too late. Bob thought Stan sent the check. Stan thought Bob sent the check. And, you know, the more time that goes by in these cases, the worse off the title company could be, the new buyer could be. So, just to kind of give yourself a little tickler if you're running up against these redemption dates. Hey, let me look into this now in two weeks and 3 weeks and actually make sure those taxes are redeemed and get proof of that so that way I can, you know, assure my client they don't have an issue there. >> Gotcha. And as for your clients, if if if their involvement in the tax enforcement system is sunseted, what they'll just what will they pivot and they'll invest in something else and like what would happen to your practice area? You know, I I never say any, you know, I'm not a mind readader or anything like that, but as I mentioned, those other 12 states that were affected by Tyler, they they modified their statutes, most of them, towards some sort of judicial auction situation, and they still have private tax and they still have private investing. Any sunset that's currently laid out in legislative proposals is just for Cook County. So granted it is the biggest county but I do think that there is still a need and there still will be a place for private investing in tax buying in Illinois. And then again with the practice area it might contract a little bit um and you know we might have to find you know some new side things to do but I do think there is still um in this enforcement procedure with real estate taxes still a need for attorneys that kind of concentrate in this area. Gotcha. So, just to sum it up, what's your advice for anybody that would think about getting involved in investing in tax deeds and tax sale process right now? >> Right now, I wouldn't do it. [laughter] I do have clients that sometimes come, you know, wanting to, you know, the a lot of these certificates are assigned between parties. Um, I I wouldn't necessarily advise for that at this juncture just because of the season we're in with these. and Tyler. Um, you you could potentially being be be buying liability. As you mentioned, we do have class action lawsuits against some of these county individuals, but now we're seeing state court class actions where it's homeowners suing now these tax buyers. So, we're still very much in a gray area with all of this. Um, and I would just hope that the legislature kind of whatever the decision is that is made, um, that some sort of legislative actions taken to kind of move the process along. >> All right, sounds good.
